#### Extended field 01 — Premise and canon

The floodline watch exchange begins as a premise audit around Red Lantern Horizon. The player is asked to compare two damaged records, but the proposal remains provisional until current source, JSON authority, event producer, host consumer, and ownership ledger are cited. Record the nearest existing seam, the exact absent seam, and the collision to exclude. If the premise is already represented, fold the prose into that owner and retire this packet rather than creating a duplicate.

#### Extended field 02 — Player loop

The loop has six readable beats: arrive at Red Lantern Horizon, inspect a practical sign, hear a resident’s account, choose a cost, perform one visible task, and return after the next weather or duty turn. The choice can preserve, delay, redirect, or refuse the request. Show the consequence before explanation. A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for endgame horizons and legacy frontiers. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. The packet may touch faction standing, route access, roster duty, shelter archive, relationship, expedition, or ending interpretation only through those authorities. It may not create a private truce score, route graph, calendar, inventory, reputation counter, or parallel legacy record.

#### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The mechanic should have a threshold, a visible cost, a reversible preparation state, and a deterministic result. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

At Slate Orchard Beacon, describe who built the room, which flood or fire altered it, who kept the key, and why one wall remains unpainted. Give the player a physical trace, a remembered phrase, a disputed interpretation, and a maintenance action. Returning to the site should show an object moved, repaired, withheld, or shared before any dialogue summarizes the change.

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Slate Orchard Beacon notices labor and weather. A representative of Red Lantern Horizon Authority speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to South Badger Assembly remembers a different sequence. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive a measurable roster, route, archive, or ending consequence.

#### Extended field 08 — Faction politics

The faction layer distinguishes Red Lantern Horizon Authority, South Badger Assembly, Slate Orchard Witnesses, and Cobalt Rain Custodians by resource, ritual, and risk rather than color. Red Lantern Horizon Authority wants a reliable public record, South Badger Assembly protects a route custom, Slate Orchard Witnesses values a scarce repair skill, and Cobalt Rain Custodians demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

#### Extended field 09 — Story and prose

The side quest opens with an ordinary sentence: someone asks whether the lamp, map, ledger, meal, or signal can wait one more night. The player’s answer changes who performs the task and what is remembered. Use restrained prose, concrete objects, and one silence that another character interprets differently. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants.

#### Extended field 10 — Late-game system

The late-game form is a major faction or frontier institution that can only appear after several owner-bound facts agree. It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

#### Extended field 11 — Data and catalog

Candidate content rows for floodline watch exchange carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Link every row to one canonical consumer and one command. Keep Cobalt Rain Frontier, South Badger Causeway, Slate Orchard Witnesses, and Cobalt Rain Custodians provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven.

#### Extended field 12 — Save and migration

Use the smallest existing save section. Capture the new fact, restore it, migrate older envelopes, tolerate an absent optional row, and make duplicate events idempotent. Define the pre-event, committed, refused, interrupted, and restored states. Do not encode prose branches in a panel cache. A rollback note must identify the event boundary and the owner responsible for undo or compensating projection.

#### Extended field 13 — Deterministic replay

Pin seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation. Avoid wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, hidden random choices, and locale-sensitive sorting. Include a late-arrival replay and a missing-record replay so optional content cannot alter the deterministic core unexpectedly.

#### Extended field 14 — UI and accessibility

The UI exposes a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard and controller back behavior, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, and confirmation for irreversible choices. Provide an audio or text alternative. If a record is missing, show a truthful unavailable state and preserve navigation. Archive and map panels consume projections; they do not own decisions.

#### Extended field 15 — Performance and lifecycle

Set budgets for catalog parse, query, event dispatch, archive projection, panel refresh, long text, and return visits. Load high-volume rows lazily, page them without changing order, dispose listeners on close, and avoid repeated full-catalog scans. Add one degradation path for a missing asset or provider. Note the smallest focused host smoke needed if the owner route is eventually implemented.

#### Extended field 16 — Acceptance and handoff

Acceptance requires premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable player command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and a rollback boundary. The handoff names untouched shared paths and labels this as design scaffolding. The final image is practical: a repaired latch, an amended map, a divided bowl, a chalk mark, a quiet signal, or a door left open by consent.

### Wave 51 capsule 01: double-signature arbitration at Red Lantern Horizon

**Opening and choice.** At **Red Lantern Horizon**, the player finds a practical problem that cannot be solved by rhetoric alone: a weather window is closing, a shared tool has two claimants, a missing person may be returning, a night signal is being misread, an apprentice is ready before the shelter is ready, a water ration has been counted twice, a quiet route carries an old debt, or a legacy object must be placed in another person’s hands. The player inspects the evidence, asks for consent, compares accounts, chooses a cost, defers, or leaves. The cost appears before commitment and a refusal keeps a safe return path.

**Authority and mechanic.** Route the action through the current owner for endgame horizons and legacy frontiers. Define one command, one event key, one resulting fact, one refusal result, one fallback, and one idempotency rule. A derived readiness view may combine existing standing, relationship, route, roster, shelter, archive, expedition, or ending facts, but it cannot become a second ledger or clock. The mechanic should make an ordinary task consequential: rescheduling a crossing changes who carries a tool, recording a signal changes which watch is asked to stand, or accepting a handover changes who is invited to the next meeting. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk version first.

**Place and shelter lore.** At **Slate Orchard Beacon**, describe the builder, the repair that saved the room, the person who still pays for that repair, and the mark that remains unexplained. At **Cobalt Rain Frontier**, place a contrasting trace: a patched hinge, a dry shelf, an erased route line, a bell rope, a teaching slate, or a bowl set aside. At **South Badger Causeway**, let a shelter custom make the history useful: a lamp is moved only after consent, a tool is returned sharpened, a guest cup is washed before dawn, or a route name is spoken once and then left unclaimed. Returning to the location shows a changed object before exposition.

**Characters and factions.** A resident speaks in concrete duties and notices who will carry the burden. A representative of **Red Lantern Horizon Authority** uses public language and wants an auditable result. A voice from **South Badger Assembly** protects a custom that looks inefficient until its history is heard. **Slate Orchard Witnesses** values a scarce skill, while **Cobalt Rain Custodians** asks who will witness the consequence after the player leaves. Give each voice a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and callback. The late-game factional version may convene a coalition, certify a passage, steward a shelter custom, or preserve a memory, but it may request and witness only through existing authorities.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

## Wave 51 late-game faction and playable arc dossier — The Horizon Witness Assembly

**Canon status.** The Horizon Witness Assembly is a proposed major late-game faction, not an established catalog entity. Search the current narrative catalog, previous plan index, ownership ledger, and integration queue before implementation. If its role duplicates an existing organization, merge the useful quest material into that owner or retire this faction. The locations, leaders, mechanics, and story outcomes in this dossier remain provisional.

### Mandate and opening incident

A late-game assembly that may coordinate a final evidence hearing, sponsor a voluntary crossing or remain-in-place plan, and preserve competing interpretations for the existing ending/legacy resolver. It cannot add an ending counter, declare a canon ending, or create a parallel campaign authority. At Last Beacon a signal arrives with half the expected call sign and a familiar pause. Edda recognizes the pause but will not claim the sender. Kell wants to answer before the window closes. The player can verify the carrier record, request a repeat, send a noncommittal acknowledgment, or let the window pass. The first scene teaches that endgame certainty is a choice about evidence and responsibility, not a glowing final switch.

### Five-quest playable spine

Quest 1 — The Half Call: compare the incoming signal with existing radio/archive records and decide whether uncertainty belongs in the journal. Quest 2 — Names for the Thaw Camp: ask residents at New Thaw Camps whether the map should preserve a temporary name or omit it. Quest 3 — The Gate without a Charter: at Long Glass Gate, negotiate a safety inspection and a voluntary departure window without promising safety the team cannot prove. Quest 4 — A Future Kept Local: Kell and Edda disagree over whether to broadcast a frontier plan; the player can offer a private route briefing or a public invitation. Quest 5 — The Last Hearing: the Assembly reads only campaign, faction, expedition, shelter, relationship, and archive facts already owned by their systems, then offers accept, refuse, defer, or leave unresolved. Epilogue callbacks vary by what the player actually did: the beacon continues, goes quiet, or answers with a limited phrase.

### Faction structure and late-game function

The Assembly’s internal constituencies are the Returners, who prioritize a safe path back; the Keepers, who value continuity at existing shelters; and the Open Horizon group, who want a voluntary frontier attempt. Each has a valid fear and a finite supply argument. The late game does not score the player’s morality. It presents practical evidence, consent, and tradeoffs, allowing an ending projection to interpret the combined facts through the current resolver. The faction becomes available only when required existing facts are present; its entry point is a hearing, not a new menu unlocked by hidden points. A campaign that lacks the signal, route, or shelter conditions can still reach the ending through existing routes. The Assembly may request that the player publish the uncertainty, carry the message physically, or leave the channel silent. This can alter which existing epilogue text is eligible only if the current ending contract supports it; otherwise it remains optional narrative content and the ending output stays unchanged.

### Named character personalities

Edda records what she heard, then marks which part she inferred. Kell speaks in plans because silence feels like a vote to abandon the frontier. A third character, Suri Dane, stayed behind during an earlier evacuation and resents being cast as proof for either side. Edda’s arc is learning that uncertainty can be shared without being hidden; Kell learns to ask who wants to travel; Suri tells the player which version of the story she is willing to have archived. None is a mascot for an ending choice.

### Diegetic prose and scene variants

Prose fragments: “The signal ended where a name should have been.” “Kell folded the route sheet along the old crease, then stopped before tearing it.” “Suri asked for her own sentence to remain beside the Assembly’s conclusion.” Variants should preserve silence and uncertainty: a blank transmission, a repeat call, a late return, a refusal to travel, or an empty beacon room. Give each variant a clear factual state and a compact, optional narrative reading.

### Existing-system contract, save, and replay

The ending and legacy resolver remains the sole authority. The Assembly consumes existing facts and emits, at most, an event or archive item explicitly supported by current contracts. It does not store a second convergence state, calculate a moral score, or override old saves. Any optional endgame row must have a missing-content fallback and deterministic eligibility. The migration test should load a pre-Assembly save and prove that the existing epilogue remains valid without adding this faction.

### UI, accessibility, performance, and acceptance

The endgame interface shows known facts, disputed facts, withheld facts, travel risks, shelter alternatives, and the consequences of waiting. A comparison view makes no choice on behalf of the player. The player may leave and return without losing their place. Keyboard/controller input must support “send limited reply,” “keep local,” “defer,” and “decline.” Performance work must avoid recomputing the whole campaign projection on every dialog open. All elements remain provisional until the ending owner, archive consumer, and current claims are checked.

**Promotion boundary.** The faction becomes implementation-ready only after a current-source premise check names its owner, consumer, event producer, data schema, save path if stateful, host route, and rollback seam. No faction name or narrative outcome here is canon until that review is complete.

## Wave 52 supplemental receipt

The supplemental packets preserve the active twenty-field structure and broaden the playable content bank. They remain provisional until current catalog, ownership, save, replay, UI, accessibility, performance, and rollback evidence is attached.


## Wave 52 extended depth layer

This larger tranche adds six extended packets per plan. They deepen the active twenty fields while keeping all mechanics, catalog rows, factions, locations, shelter customs, and late-game institutions provisional and owner-bound.

### Wave 52 extended depth packet 01: two-seal petition compact at Red Lantern Horizon

#### Extended field 01 — Premise and canon

The two-seal petition compact begins as a premise audit around Red Lantern Horizon. The player is asked to count the lamps before opening the door, but the proposal remains provisional until current source, JSON authority, event producer, host consumer, and ownership ledger are cited. Record the nearest existing seam, the exact absent seam, and the collision to exclude. If the premise is already represented, fold the prose into that owner and retire this packet rather than creating a duplicate.

#### Extended field 02 — Player loop

The loop has six readable beats: arrive at Red Lantern Horizon, inspect a practical sign, hear a resident’s account, choose a cost, perform one visible task, and return after the next weather or duty turn. The choice can preserve, delay, redirect, or refuse the request. Show the consequence before explanation. A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for endgame horizons and legacy frontiers. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. The packet may touch faction standing, route access, roster duty, shelter archive, relationship, expedition, or ending interpretation only through those authorities. It may not create a private truce score, route graph, calendar, inventory, reputation counter, or parallel legacy record.

#### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The mechanic should have a threshold, a visible cost, a reversible preparation state, and a deterministic result. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

At Slate Orchard Beacon, describe who built the room, which flood or fire altered it, who kept the key, and why one wall remains unpainted. Give the player a physical trace, a remembered phrase, a disputed interpretation, and a maintenance action. Returning to the site should show an object moved, repaired, withheld, or shared before any dialogue summarizes the change.

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Slate Orchard Beacon notices labor and weather. A representative of Red Lantern Horizon Authority speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to South Badger Assembly remembers a different sequence. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive a measurable roster, route, archive, or ending consequence.

#### Extended field 08 — Faction politics

The faction layer distinguishes Red Lantern Horizon Authority, South Badger Assembly, Slate Orchard Witnesses, and Cobalt Rain Custodians by resource, ritual, and risk rather than color. Red Lantern Horizon Authority wants a reliable public record, South Badger Assembly protects a route custom, Slate Orchard Witnesses values a scarce repair skill, and Cobalt Rain Custodians demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

#### Extended field 09 — Story and prose

The side quest opens with an ordinary sentence: someone asks whether the lamp, map, ledger, meal, or signal can wait one more night. The player’s answer changes who performs the task and what is remembered. Use restrained prose, concrete objects, and one silence that another character interprets differently. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants.

#### Extended field 10 — Late-game system

The late-game form is a major faction or frontier institution that can only appear after several owner-bound facts agree. It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

#### Extended field 11 — Data and catalog

Candidate content rows for two-seal petition compact carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Link every row to one canonical consumer and one command. Keep Cobalt Rain Frontier, South Badger Causeway, Slate Orchard Witnesses, and Cobalt Rain Custodians provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven.

#### Extended field 12 — Save and migration

Use the smallest existing save section. Capture the new fact, restore it, migrate older envelopes, tolerate an absent optional row, and make duplicate events idempotent. Define the pre-event, committed, refused, interrupted, and restored states. Do not encode prose branches in a panel cache. A rollback note must identify the event boundary and the owner responsible for undo or compensating projection.

#### Extended field 13 — Deterministic replay

Pin seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation. Avoid wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, hidden random choices, and locale-sensitive sorting. Include a late-arrival replay and a missing-record replay so optional content cannot alter the deterministic core unexpectedly.

#### Extended field 14 — UI and accessibility

The UI exposes a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard and controller back behavior, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, and confirmation for irreversible choices. Provide an audio or text alternative. If a record is missing, show a truthful unavailable state and preserve navigation. Archive and map panels consume projections; they do not own decisions.

#### Extended field 15 — Performance and lifecycle

Set budgets for catalog parse, query, event dispatch, archive projection, panel refresh, long text, and return visits. Load high-volume rows lazily, page them without changing order, dispose listeners on close, and avoid repeated full-catalog scans. Add one degradation path for a missing asset or provider. ### Wave 52 capsule 01: double-signature arbitration at Red Lantern Horizon

**Opening and choice.** At **Red Lantern Horizon**, the player finds a practical problem that cannot be solved by rhetoric alone: a weather window is closing, a shared tool has two claimants, a missing person may be returning, a night signal is being misread, an apprentice is ready before the shelter is ready, a water ration has been counted twice, a quiet route carries an old debt, or a legacy object must be placed in another person’s hands. The player inspects the evidence, asks for consent, compares accounts, chooses a cost, defers, or leaves. The cost appears before commitment and a refusal keeps a safe return path.

**Authority and mechanic.** Route the action through the current owner for endgame horizons and legacy frontiers. Define one command, one event key, one resulting fact, one refusal result, one fallback, and one idempotency rule. A derived readiness view may combine existing standing, relationship, route, roster, shelter, archive, expedition, or ending facts, but it cannot become a second ledger or clock. The mechanic should make an ordinary task consequential: rescheduling a crossing changes who carries a tool, recording a signal changes which watch is asked to stand, or accepting a handover changes who is invited to the next meeting. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk version first.

**Place and shelter lore.** At **Slate Orchard Beacon**, describe the builder, the repair that saved the room, the person who still pays for that repair, and the mark that remains unexplained. At **Cobalt Rain Frontier**, place a contrasting trace: a patched hinge, a dry shelf, an erased route line, a bell rope, a teaching slate, or a bowl set aside. At **South Badger Causeway**, let a shelter custom make the history useful: a lamp is moved only after consent, a tool is returned sharpened, a guest cup is washed before dawn, or a route name is spoken once and then left unclaimed. Returning to the location shows a changed object before exposition.

**Characters and factions.** A resident speaks in concrete duties and notices who will carry the burden. A representative of **Red Lantern Horizon Authority** uses public language and wants an auditable result. A voice from **South Badger Assembly** protects a custom that looks inefficient until its history is heard. **Slate Orchard Witnesses** values a scarce skill, while **Cobalt Rain Custodians** asks who will witness the consequence after the player leaves. Give each voice a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and callback. The late-game factional version may convene a coalition, certify a passage, steward a shelter custom, or preserve a memory, but it may request and witness only through existing authorities.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

**Data and content volume.** Candidate rows carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Create arrival, inspection, task, hazard, rest, departure, return, calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, and late-arrival variants. Keep the names of **Red Lantern Horizon Authority**, **South Badger Assembly**, **Slate Orchard Witnesses**, and **Cobalt Rain Custodians** provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven. A missing optional row should collapse to a truthful unavailable state rather than alter the deterministic core.

**Persistence and replay.** Capture the smallest new fact through the existing save section. Define pre-action, committed, refused, interrupted, restored, migrated, and duplicate-event states. Pin the campaign seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation, including the late-arrival and missing-record cases. Do not use wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, locale-sensitive sorting, or hidden randomness in prose.

**UI, accessibility, and lifecycle.** Expose a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard/controller close and back, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, confirmation for irreversible actions, and text or audio alternatives. Panels consume owner projections and dispose listeners on close. High-volume rows load lazily and page without changing order. Set budgets for parse, query, dispatch, archive projection, refresh, and return visits; document the missing-provider path and the smallest eventual host smoke.

**Acceptance and handoff.** Accept the capsule only with premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and rollback. The handoff records untouched shared paths and labels the content as design scaffolding. The final image is small and physical: a cord retied, a cup passed over, a map corrected, a signal answered, a tool returned sharper, a meal divided, or a door left open because someone was asked first.

## Wave 52 late-game faction and playable arc dossier — The Return-Sure League

**Canon and collision status.** The Return-Sure League is proposed major late-game content, not an established faction. Its role must be compared with current catalog records, source owners, live plan index, integration queue, and path claims. If it duplicates a current faction, archive, route, education, or ending contract, merge its usable quests into that authority or retire the proposal. Locations, characters, and outcomes remain provisional.

### Mandate and opening incident at Far Signal

The Return-Sure League is a proposed late-game expedition faction whose members insist that every outward plan show a credible return option, a support burden, and a point at which the expedition can be called off. It does not own vehicles, routes, supply, or the ending. It convenes pilots, shelter stewards, and families to inspect the plan with current expedition and campaign projections. Its conflict is between preserving the chance to leave and preserving a path back for those who choose to return. At Far Signal, a board lists three frontier destinations and one route home. The route home has no current inspection date. One pilot says the old check is good enough; a shelter keeper says the weather changed after it was recorded. The player can ask for a new inspection, preserve the old plan but mark it uncertain, select a shorter trial, or refuse departure. The faction’s first lesson is that “return possible” is a claim with an owner and a date, not a reassurance.

### Five-quest story spine

Quest 1 — The Missing Inspection: follow the route reference to the last verified point and determine whether the inspection fact still belongs to the current map. Quest 2 — Who Carries the Return Kit: at New Census Camp, compare the expedition list with the shelter’s actual capacity; do not silently duplicate resources. Quest 3 — A Pilot’s Refusal: meet the pilot at Bright Causeway and let them refuse a route without turning refusal into a personal failure flag. Quest 4 — The Family That Stays: discuss the departure plan with people who choose to remain; give them a meaningful shelter-support option. Quest 5 — The Return-Sure Hearing: at Long Winter Gate, choose launch, delay, local trial, or abandon. Each outcome changes only existing campaign/expedition/legacy projections when supported. The late callback shows the return board updated, crossed out, or left with a blank inspection field.

### Faction tensions and late-game leverage

The Route Testers ask for fresh field evidence; the Long Stay families want supplies kept at shelters; the First Step pilots argue that a small trial can answer what a map cannot. The League’s major-faction role is to make these costs visible before the final frontier choice. It cannot veto the player, guarantee survival, or declare that staying is cowardice. Each branch preserves meaningful play after refusing departure. The faction’s practical strength comes from convening people who already have authority over the relevant task. Its leverage is a credible witness, a better-timed request, or an option to defer; it gains no hidden territory, reputation track, clock, inventory pool, or ending state. A player can refuse membership and still complete the surrounding story.

### Character voices and relationships

Aren Vey, a pilot, makes dry jokes when nervous and stops speaking when someone calls a route safe without saying who checked it. Lio Marr, a shelter steward, dislikes being asked to represent everyone who stays. Emet Sol, a young surveyor, wants to go but admits that they have not asked their sibling. Each character’s position may shift, but none becomes a proxy for the player’s morality. Recurring dialogue should show this through changed duties and everyday habits: who gets asked first, who moves a cup, who checks a latch, who gets an uninterrupted turn to speak. Relationship consequences are routed through the existing relationship owner; avoid numerical affinity gates invented for this faction.

### Prose and playable variation

Prose lines: “The route home was drawn in darker ink. It was older ink.” “Aren circled the inspection date, not the destination.” “Lio asked the room who had been counted as cargo last time.” Use concrete expedition tools, quiet disagreements, and callbacks based on the actual choice. Include “return later,” “send no answer,” “short trial,” “launch,” and “remain” variants with no hidden failure for staying. Author scene variants for ordinary conditions, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late arrival, missing evidence, and changed relationships. Keep each variant tied to one observable event or prop. Side quests should expose costs and agency before interpreting the choice. Do not make lore access depend on accepting the faction’s interpretation.

### New feature and system proposal

The new feature proposal is a return-readiness review that composes current route, vehicle, expedition, roster, supply, and shelter projections. It introduces no readiness score or hidden resource reserve. An optional review result can be “verified,” “stale,” “unknown,” or “declined,” but any persisted status must belong to a current owner; if no owner exists, present it only within the scene. The UnifiedEndingResolver and CampaignLegacySystem remain the only ending authorities. The proposal should be implemented as content and projection over existing owners unless a future architecture decision explicitly authorizes a new owner. Describe command, event, consumer, save contract if stateful, migration, deterministic replay, and rollback before data is added. If the necessary premise is absent, retain the design note and omit mutable state.

### UI, accessibility, performance, and verification

The interface places outward and return legs side by side, shows source and inspection recency, names the crew burden, and marks unknowns with text rather than color alone. The player can compare plans, open the source, ask the crew, choose a trial, defer, or cancel. Keyboard/controller focus supports all alternatives. Paging prevents a long frontier catalog from loading at once. Acceptance includes old-save behavior, replay of the same choice set, missing-route fallback, accessible map labels, bounded projection cost, and explicit collision/ownership review. The dossier is ready for implementation review only after evidence identifies exact source paths, API or data families, event producers, host routes, save owners, and unclaimed implementation paths. Test only the focused owner contract, data validator, save round-trip, and deterministic replay that the approved seam requires. No full suite is implied by this plan.

## Wave 53 supplemental receipt

The supplemental packets preserve the active twenty-field structure and broaden the playable content bank. They remain provisional until current catalog, ownership, save, replay, UI, accessibility, performance, and rollback evidence is attached.


## Wave 53 extended depth layer

This larger tranche adds six extended packets per plan. They deepen the active twenty fields while keeping all mechanics, catalog rows, factions, locations, shelter customs, and late-game institutions provisional and owner-bound.

### Wave 53 extended depth packet 01: copperline witness table at Red Lantern Horizon

#### Extended field 01 — Premise and canon

The copperline witness table begins as a premise audit around Red Lantern Horizon. The player is asked to count the lamps before opening the door, but the proposal remains provisional until current source, JSON authority, event producer, host consumer, and ownership ledger are cited. Record the nearest existing seam, the exact absent seam, and the collision to exclude. If the premise is already represented, fold the prose into that owner and retire this packet rather than creating a duplicate.

#### Extended field 02 — Player loop

The loop has six readable beats: arrive at Red Lantern Horizon, inspect a practical sign, hear a resident’s account, choose a cost, perform one visible task, and return after the next weather or duty turn. The choice can preserve, delay, redirect, or refuse the request. Show the consequence before explanation. A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for endgame horizons and legacy frontiers. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. The packet may touch faction standing, route access, roster duty, shelter archive, relationship, expedition, or ending interpretation only through those authorities. It may not create a private truce score, route graph, calendar, inventory, reputation counter, or parallel legacy record.

#### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The mechanic should have a threshold, a visible cost, a reversible preparation state, and a deterministic result. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

At Slate Orchard Beacon, describe who built the room, which flood or fire altered it, who kept the key, and why one wall remains unpainted. Give the player a physical trace, a remembered phrase, a disputed interpretation, and a maintenance action. Returning to the site should show an object moved, repaired, withheld, or shared before any dialogue summarizes the change.

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Slate Orchard Beacon notices labor and weather. A representative of Red Lantern Horizon Authority speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to South Badger Assembly remembers a different sequence. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive a measurable roster, route, archive, or ending consequence.

#### Extended field 08 — Faction politics

The faction layer distinguishes Red Lantern Horizon Authority, South Badger Assembly, Slate Orchard Witnesses, and Cobalt Rain Custodians by resource, ritual, and risk rather than color. Red Lantern Horizon Authority wants a reliable public record, South Badger Assembly protects a route custom, Slate Orchard Witnesses values a scarce repair skill, and Cobalt Rain Custodians demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

#### Extended field 09 — Story and prose

The side quest opens with an ordinary sentence: someone asks whether the lamp, map, ledger, meal, or signal can wait one more night. The player’s answer changes who performs the task and what is remembered. Use restrained prose, concrete objects, and one silence that another character interprets differently. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants.

#### Extended field 10 — Late-game system

The late-game form is a major faction or frontier institution that can only appear after several owner-bound facts agree. It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

#### Extended field 11 — Data and catalog

It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

#### Extended field 11 — Data and catalog

Candidate content rows for return signal charter carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Link every row to one canonical consumer and one command. Keep Cobalt Rain Frontier, South Badger Causeway, Slate Orchard Witnesses, and Cobalt Rain Custodians provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven.

#### Extended field 12 — Save and migration

Use the smallest existing save section. Capture the new fact, restore it, migrate older envelopes, tolerate an absent optional row, and make duplicate events idempotent. Define the pre-event, committed, refused, interrupted, and restored states. Do not encode prose branches in a panel cache. A rollback note must identify the event boundary and the owner responsible for undo or compensating projection.

#### Extended field 13 — Deterministic replay

Pin seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation. Avoid wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, hidden random choices, and locale-sensitive sorting. Include a late-arrival replay and a missing-record replay so optional content cannot alter the deterministic core unexpectedly.

#### Extended field 14 — UI and accessibility

The UI exposes a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard and controller back behavior, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, and confirmation for irreversible choices. Provide an audio or text alternative. If a record is missing, show a truthful unavailable state and preserve navigation. Archive and map panels consume projections; they do not own decisions.

#### Extended field 15 — Performance and lifecycle

Set budgets for catalog parse, query, event dispatch, archive projection, panel refresh, long text, and return visits. Load high-volume rows lazily, page them without changing order, dispose listeners on close, and avoid repeated full-catalog scans. Add one degradation path for a missing asset or provider. Note the smallest focused host smoke needed if the owner route is eventually implemented.

#### Extended field 16 — Acceptance and handoff

Acceptance requires premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable player command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and a rollback boundary. The handoff names untouched shared paths and labels this as design scaffolding. The final image is practical: a repaired latch, an amended map, a divided bowl, a chalk mark, a quiet signal, or a door left open by consent.

## Wave 53 extended depth receipt

The extended layer is documentation-only. Promotion requires current premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, reachable content, deterministic persistence and replay, accessibility, performance, and rollback evidence.


## Wave 53 capsule layer

These capsules extend the Wave 53 fields with additional playable scaffolds. Each remains provisional, owner-bound, and documentation-only.

### Wave 53 capsule 01: empty bowl reconciliation at Red Lantern Horizon

**Opening and choice.** At **Red Lantern Horizon**, the player finds a practical problem that cannot be solved by rhetoric alone: a weather window is closing, a shared tool has two claimants, a missing person may be returning, a night signal is being misread, an apprentice is ready before the shelter is ready, a water ration has been counted twice, a quiet route carries an old debt, or a legacy object must be placed in another person’s hands. The player inspects the evidence, asks for consent, compares accounts, chooses a cost, defers, or leaves. The cost appears before commitment and a refusal keeps a safe return path.

**Authority and mechanic.** Route the action through the current owner for endgame horizons and legacy frontiers. Define one command, one event key, one resulting fact, one refusal result, one fallback, and one idempotency rule. A derived readiness view may combine existing standing, relationship, route, roster, shelter, archive, expedition, or ending facts, but it cannot become a second ledger or clock. The mechanic should make an ordinary task consequential: rescheduling a crossing changes who carries a tool, recording a signal changes which watch is asked to stand, or accepting a handover changes who is invited to the next meeting. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk version first.

**Place and shelter lore.** At **Slate Orchard Beacon**, describe the builder, the repair that saved the room, the person who still pays for that repair, and the mark that remains unexplained. At **Cobalt Rain Frontier**, place a contrasting trace: a patched hinge, a dry shelf, an erased route line, a bell rope, a teaching slate, or a bowl set aside. At **South Badger Causeway**, let a shelter custom make the history useful: a lamp is moved only after consent, a tool is returned sharpened, a guest cup is washed before dawn, or a route name is spoken once and then left unclaimed. Returning to the location shows a changed object before exposition.

**Characters and factions.** A resident speaks in concrete duties and notices who will carry the burden. A representative of **Red Lantern Horizon Authority** uses public language and wants an auditable result. A voice from **South Badger Assembly** protects a custom that looks inefficient until its history is heard. **Slate Orchard Witnesses** values a scarce skill, while **Cobalt Rain Custodians** asks who will witness the consequence after the player leaves. Give each voice a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and callback. The late-game factional version may convene a coalition, certify a passage, steward a shelter custom, or preserve a memory, but it may request and witness only through existing authorities.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

**Data and content volume.** Candidate rows carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Create arrival, inspection, task, hazard, rest, departure, return, calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, and late-arrival variants. Keep the names of **Red Lantern Horizon Authority**, **South Badger Assembly**, **Slate Orchard Witnesses**, and **Cobalt Rain Custodians** provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven. A missing optional row should collapse to a truthful unavailable state rather than alter the deterministic core.

**Persistence and replay.** Capture the smallest new fact through the existing save section. Define pre-action, committed, refused, interrupted, restored, migrated, and duplicate-event states. Pin the campaign seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation, including the late-arrival and missing-record cases. Do not use wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, locale-sensitive sorting, or hidden randomness in prose.

**UI, accessibility, and lifecycle.** Expose a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard/controller close and back, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, confirmation for irreversible actions, and text or audio alternatives. Panels consume owner projections and dispose listeners on close. High-volume rows load lazily and page without changing order. Set budgets for parse, query, dispatch, archive projection, refresh, and return visits; document the missing-provider path and the smallest eventual host smoke.

**Acceptance and handoff.** Accept the capsule only with premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and rollback. The handoff records untouched shared paths and labels the content as design scaffolding. The final image is small and physical: a cord retied, a cup passed over, a map corrected, a signal answered, a tool returned sharper, a meal divided, or a door left open because someone was asked first.

## Wave 53 late-game faction and playable arc dossier — The Afterweather Assembly

**Canon and collision status.** The Afterweather Assembly is a proposed major late-game faction, not an established catalog entity. Compare its story role, proper names, feature contract, and locations with current data, plans, ownership, and integration queues before promotion. If it duplicates existing work, merge the useful quest beats into the existing owner or retire this proposal.

### Mandate and opening incident at Northstar Array

The Afterweather Assembly is a proposed late-game coalition that reviews whether a frontier plan can be paused, reversed, or adapted after a major weather shift. It differs from the Return-Sure League: it focuses on what happens after the outward plan changes, not on proving a return route before departure. The Assembly can convene shelter stewards, expedition planners, and local residents to request a review of existing campaign facts. It cannot own a climate simulator, declare a canonical ending, or promise that any place is safe. At Northstar Array the morning measurement disagrees with the previous night’s forecast. A small camp is already halfway through a planned move, and the second wagon has not left. One group says the delay will strand them; another says arriving early would place people in a wet shelter. The player can pause the second trip, ask for a local check, keep the original schedule, or change only the supplies already loaded.

### Five-quest story spine

Quest 1 — The Forecast with Two Owners: identify which report came from current weather authority and which is a remembered observation. Quest 2 — The Camp That Could Wait: at Quiet Meridian Camp, ask residents whether temporary shelter or travel is their preferred option. Quest 3 — The Wagon at High Shelf Road: negotiate whether to unload one exposed supply crate before the weather turns, using current inventory and expedition commands. Quest 4 — The Shelter after the Move: learn that the receiving shelter can host people but not the workshop equipment; the player can plan a second trip or change the work plan. Quest 5 — The Afterweather Hearing: at Last Hearth Gate, the Assembly records adapt, pause, continue, or reverse as a player-directed request to existing owners. The epilogue callback reflects what the party actually did, never an abstract “wisdom” score.

### Faction conflict and late-game role

The Continuers warn that repeated pauses become abandonment; the Weather Readers say that forecasts without review dates are promises no one can keep; the Camp Residents insist that people already in motion must be asked before planners redraw the schedule. The faction’s role is to set a review ritual and preserve competing interpretations. It may advise, request, and carry an answer but cannot alter weather or travel owners. Its late-game strength is social and procedural: it can bring affected people into the same decision, make costs legible, and request actions through existing owners. It has no independent territory, resource pool, standing score, quest ledger, travel graph, or ending authority. Players may decline membership and still finish adjacent content.

### Character personalities and relationships

Talen Rho trusts measurements but knows his instruments can be wrong. Veya San lives in the camp and refuses to let a map label her family “relocated” before they choose. Oris Pell drives the wagon and dislikes being praised for taking a risk he did not consent to. Each has a concrete interest in the plan. Late-game scenes reveal that adapting can preserve a goal while changing a route, and that a pause can be an active choice rather than failure. Preserve these personalities through ordinary actions and callbacks, not exposition dumps. Relationship changes must use the current relationship owner and must not become numerical faction-affinity gates. Give a minor character the ability to refuse a public role without blocking the practical quest outcome.

### Prose and playable variants

Prose fragments: “The wind shifted the paper before it shifted the flags.” “Veya folded the map at the camp, not at the road.” “Oris checked the load straps and waited for someone to say whether the wagon was still leaving.” Include continue, pause, adapt, reverse, and refuse-to-decide variants. Each scene must show who bears the next task, what can be recovered, and which fact remains uncertain. Avoid certainty language for future weather. Author calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Keep each branch tied to an observable prop or task. A moral disagreement should not hide the resource, privacy, travel, work, or shelter cost. The player may ask, defer, accept, refuse, or leave wherever the owner contract permits.

### Feature and system proposal

The “afterweather review” is a proposed presentation and request flow over existing weather, expedition, campaign, shelter, and ending owners. It adds no climate state or ending flag. Each option submits an existing command where available; otherwise it remains narrative-only and cannot claim persistence. A review record may include source references, review reason, selected action, and owner event. The ending resolver receives only supported campaign facts. Seeded replay verifies same choices and outcomes when source facts match; old saves without the Assembly remain valid. This is a content and projection proposal over existing authorities unless a future architecture decision explicitly creates a new owner. Specify the command, event, consumer, persistence owner if stateful, migration behavior, deterministic replay, and rollback boundary before implementation. If a required API or host route does not exist, preserve this as a design question and do not create local mutable state.

### UI, accessibility, performance, and handoff

Display forecast source, time reference, observed signs, route status, receiving shelter capacity, and requested change together. Distinguish “forecast changed,” “observation disagrees,” and “unknown.” Use readable labels, non-color cues, keyboard/controller focus, reduced motion, and a clear cancel action. The player can leave and return without a hidden timer unless a current owner exposes one. Use incremental projection refresh, bounded scenario rows, and no all-campaign rescan. Acceptance requires current owner/API proof, save/migration review if stateful, replay, accessible map copy, performance measurement, and rollback. Keep long text pageable, dispose listeners when panels close, provide truthful unavailable states, and use bounded lookups rather than repeated full-catalog scans. Acceptance requires current-source premise proof, owner and consumer evidence, focused verification, accessibility review, and a collision check against active plans. All faction and content names remain provisional.

## Wave 54 extended depth layer

This larger tranche adds six extended packets per plan. They deepen the active twenty fields while keeping all mechanics, catalog rows, factions, locations, shelter customs, and late-game institutions provisional and owner-bound.

### Wave 54 extended depth packet 01: marlight promise review at Red Lantern Horizon

#### Extended field 01 — Premise and canon

The marlight promise review begins as a premise audit around Red Lantern Horizon. The player is asked to count the lamps before opening the door, but the proposal remains provisional until current source, JSON authority, event producer, host consumer, and ownership ledger are cited. Record the nearest existing seam, the exact absent seam, and the collision to exclude. If the premise is already represented, fold the prose into that owner and retire this packet rather than creating a duplicate.

#### Extended field 02 — Player loop

The loop has six readable beats: arrive at Red Lantern Horizon, inspect a practical sign, hear a resident’s account, choose a cost, perform one visible task, and return after the next weather or duty turn. The choice can preserve, delay, redirect, or refuse the request. Show the consequence before explanation. A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for endgame horizons and legacy frontiers. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. The packet may touch faction standing, route access, roster duty, shelter archive, relationship, expedition, or ending interpretation only through those authorities. It may not create a private truce score, route graph, calendar, inventory, reputation counter, or parallel legacy record.

#### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The mechanic should have a threshold, a visible cost, a reversible preparation state, and a deterministic result. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

At Slate Orchard Beacon, describe who built the room, which flood or fire altered it, who kept the key, and why one wall remains unpainted. Give the player a physical trace, a remembered phrase, a disputed interpretation, and a maintenance action. Returning to the site should show an object moved, repaired, withheld, or shared before any dialogue summarizes the change.

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Slate Orchard Beacon notices labor and weather. A representative of Red Lantern Horizon Authority speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to South Badger Assembly remembers a different sequence. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Slate Orchard Beacon notices labor and weather. A representative of Red Lantern Horizon Authority speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to South Badger Assembly remembers a different sequence. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive a measurable roster, route, archive, or ending consequence.

#### Extended field 08 — Faction politics

The faction layer distinguishes Red Lantern Horizon Authority, South Badger Assembly, Slate Orchard Witnesses, and Cobalt Rain Custodians by resource, ritual, and risk rather than color. Red Lantern Horizon Authority wants a reliable public record, South Badger Assembly protects a route custom, Slate Orchard Witnesses values a scarce repair skill, and Cobalt Rain Custodians demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

#### Extended field 09 — Story and prose

The side quest opens with an ordinary sentence: someone asks whether the lamp, map, ledger, meal, or signal can wait one more night. The player’s answer changes who performs the task and what is remembered. Use restrained prose, concrete objects, and one silence that another character interprets differently. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants.

#### Extended field 10 — Late-game system

The late-game form is a major faction or frontier institution that can only appear after several owner-bound facts agree. It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

#### Extended field 11 — Data and catalog

Candidate content rows for local-stay charter carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Link every row to one canonical consumer and one command. Keep Cobalt Rain Frontier, South Badger Causeway, Slate Orchard Witnesses, and Cobalt Rain Custodians provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven.

#### Extended field 12 — Save and migration

Use the smallest existing save section. Capture the new fact, restore it, migrate older envelopes, tolerate an absent optional row, and make duplicate events idempotent. Define the pre-event, committed, refused, interrupted, and restored states. Do not encode prose branches in a panel cache. A rollback note must identify the event boundary and the owner responsible for undo or compensating projection.

#### Extended field 13 — Deterministic replay

Pin seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation. Avoid wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, hidden random choices, and locale-sensitive sorting. Include a late-arrival replay and a missing-record replay so optional content cannot alter the deterministic core unexpectedly.

#### Extended field 14 — UI and accessibility

The UI exposes a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard and controller back behavior, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, and confirmation for irreversible choices. Provide an audio or text alternative. If a record is missing, show a truthful unavailable state and preserve navigation. Archive and map panels consume projections; they do not own decisions.

#### Extended field 15 — Performance and lifecycle

Set budgets for catalog parse, query, event dispatch, archive projection, panel refresh, long text, and return visits. Load high-volume rows lazily, page them without changing order, dispose listeners on close, and avoid repeated full-catalog scans. Add one degradation path for a missing asset or provider. Note the smallest focused host smoke needed if the owner route is eventually implemented.

#### Extended field 16 — Acceptance and handoff

Acceptance requires premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable player command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and a rollback boundary. The handoff names untouched shared paths and labels this as design scaffolding. The final image is practical: a repaired latch, an amended map, a divided bowl, a chalk mark, a quiet signal, or a door left open by consent.

## Wave 54 extended depth receipt

## Wave 54 capsule layer

These capsules extend the Wave 54 fields with additional playable scaffolds. Each remains provisional, owner-bound, and documentation-only.

### Wave 54 capsule 01: deferred promise review at Red Lantern Horizon

**Opening and choice.** At **Red Lantern Horizon**, the player finds a practical problem that cannot be solved by rhetoric alone: a weather window is closing, a shared tool has two claimants, a missing person may be returning, a night signal is being misread, an apprentice is ready before the shelter is ready, a water ration has been counted twice, a quiet route carries an old debt, or a legacy object must be placed in another person’s hands. The player inspects the evidence, asks for consent, compares accounts, chooses a cost, defers, or leaves. The cost appears before commitment and a refusal keeps a safe return path.

**Authority and mechanic.** Route the action through the current owner for endgame horizons and legacy frontiers. Define one command, one event key, one resulting fact, one refusal result, one fallback, and one idempotency rule. A derived readiness view may combine existing standing, relationship, route, roster, shelter, archive, expedition, or ending facts, but it cannot become a second ledger or clock. The mechanic should make an ordinary task consequential: rescheduling a crossing changes who carries a tool, recording a signal changes which watch is asked to stand, or accepting a handover changes who is invited to the next meeting. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk version first.

**Place and shelter lore.** At **Slate Orchard Beacon**, describe the builder, the repair that saved the room, the person who still pays for that repair, and the mark that remains unexplained. At **Cobalt Rain Frontier**, place a contrasting trace: a patched hinge, a dry shelf, an erased route line, a bell rope, a teaching slate, or a bowl set aside. At **South Badger Causeway**, let a shelter custom make the history useful: a lamp is moved only after consent, a tool is returned sharpened, a guest cup is washed before dawn, or a route name is spoken once and then left unclaimed. Returning to the location shows a changed object before exposition.

**Characters and factions.** A resident speaks in concrete duties and notices who will carry the burden. A representative of **Red Lantern Horizon Authority** uses public language and wants an auditable result. A voice from **South Badger Assembly** protects a custom that looks inefficient until its history is heard. **Slate Orchard Witnesses** values a scarce skill, while **Cobalt Rain Custodians** asks who will witness the consequence after the player leaves. Give each voice a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and callback. The late-game factional version may convene a coalition, certify a passage, steward a shelter custom, or preserve a memory, but it may request and witness only through existing authorities.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

**Data and content volume.** Candidate rows carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Create arrival, inspection, task, hazard, rest, departure, return, calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, and late-arrival variants. Keep the names of **Red Lantern Horizon Authority**, **South Badger Assembly**, **Slate Orchard Witnesses**, and **Cobalt Rain Custodians** provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven. A missing optional row should collapse to a truthful unavailable state rather than alter the deterministic core.

**Persistence and replay.** Capture the smallest new fact through the existing save section. Define pre-action, committed, refused, interrupted, restored, migrated, and duplicate-event states. Pin the campaign seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation, including the late-arrival and missing-record cases. Do not use wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, locale-sensitive sorting, or hidden randomness in prose.

**UI, accessibility, and lifecycle.** Expose a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard/controller close and back, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, confirmation for irreversible actions, and text or audio alternatives. Panels consume owner projections and dispose listeners on close. High-volume rows load lazily and page without changing order. Set budgets for parse, query, dispatch, archive projection, refresh, and return visits; document the missing-provider path and the smallest eventual host smoke.

**Acceptance and handoff.** Accept the capsule only with premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and rollback. The handoff records untouched shared paths and labels the content as design scaffolding. The final image is small and physical: a cord retied, a cup passed over, a map corrected, a signal answered, a tool returned sharper, a meal divided, or a door left open because someone was asked first.

## Wave 54 late-game faction and playable arc dossier — The Hearthline Assembly

**Canon and collision status.** The Hearthline Assembly is a proposed major late-game faction, not an established catalog entity. Compare the name, feature, quest spine, and data shape with current source, narrative catalogs, existing plans, live ownership, and integration queue. If it duplicates a current organization or system contract, fold the strongest quest beats into that owner or retire the proposal. All locations and faction outcomes remain provisional.

### Mandate and opening incident at Dawn Array

The Hearthline Assembly is a proposed late-game faction for communities that choose to remain at or near their current shelter while the campaign’s larger future changes around them. It plans continuity of water, shelter duty, skill handoff, and contact with departing groups. It is distinct from a return-route or weather-review faction: its concern is local life after the headline decision. It has no independent resource pool, future clock, or ending resolver. At Dawn Array a departure notice is being read aloud while the kitchen continues its usual meal rhythm. A shelter resident asks who will tend the pump after the most experienced operator leaves. Another says the question is being used to pressure everyone into staying. The player can ask for a voluntary continuity plan, invite a successor to observe, choose not to plan yet, or take the departure notice to a private room.

### Five-quest playable spine

Quest 1 — The Pump after the Farewell: ask the operator what they are willing to teach and what they will not hand over. Quest 2 — The Room That Remains: at Mile Zero Camp, residents decide which shelter space should stay open while a group travels. Quest 3 — The Contact Window: at Cloud Shelf, compare the communication plan with the actual owner-supported radio or message path; do not promise contact beyond its range. Quest 4 — The Unassigned Key: find a shelter key with no agreed successor and let residents choose whether to appoint a keeper, create a shared rotation, or leave the room closed. Quest 5 — The Hearthline Meeting: at Return Stair, choose a continuity plan that lists willing people, unresolved tasks, and a review point—or leave the plan blank. Epilogue callbacks show maintained routines only where current campaign facts support them.

### Internal conflict and late-game role

The Stay-by-Choice residents want departure to remain possible; the Continuity Stewards want essential tasks named before expertise leaves; the Open Door group refuses to let maintenance obligations become a reason to trap residents. The Assembly can convene a conversation, request a duty handoff, or preserve a voluntary plan. It cannot force survivors to stay, assign a successor, or decide the campaign ending. Staying remains a meaningful path through existing shelter and legacy owners. The faction’s reach comes from convening affected residents and making consequences visible. It can request, witness, schedule, or preserve a decision through supported current owners; it cannot seize control of the underlying mechanic. Membership is optional and never the only path to the associated quest result.

### Character personalities and recurring relationships

Olen Marr is the pump operator and wants to teach one method but not become responsible for training a whole shelter. Sava Dain is a resident who wants to stay without being praised for sacrifice. Kori Venn plans to depart and still agrees to leave one written maintenance note. Their relationships should change through requests kept or declined, not allegiance. A minor character, Nel, asks whether the key may remain unassigned until someone wants it. Personality callbacks should be expressed through who volunteers, asks permission, changes a task, or refuses a public role. Existing relationship authority owns any durable relationship consequence. Do not create a faction affinity meter to simulate character development.

### Prose and state variants

Prose fragments: “The kitchen clock kept its old hour.” “Sava asked the room not to call staying a promise.” “Kori left the key on the table beside a note that began with what might fail.” Include stay, depart, split group, defer, unassigned task, and partial handoff variations. The shelter’s lore can live in a pump checklist, a meal rota, a repaired latch, and the name residents choose for an unused bunkroom. Write concise and expanded versions, calm and pressure variants, failure and recovery, refusal, late arrival, and missing-data behavior. Keep the scene grounded in a room, route, tool, meal, signal, or duty. State clearly what the player knows, what remains disputed, and what action can still be taken.

### Proposed feature and system seam

The proposed continuity-board feature composes current roster, duty, needs, shelter, communication, campaign, and legacy projections. It does not maintain a new succession state or ending flag. Any action must route to a supported duty, journal, archive, or campaign command. If no owner can persist a handoff, keep the board as a nonpersistent meeting scene. Old saves without this faction remain valid; the UnifiedEndingResolver remains authoritative. Replay pins the same roster and campaign facts and must preserve the same stay/depart choices. This is a new content and system proposal over existing owners unless the user and foreman approve a new architecture decision. Define source facts, command, event, host route, save owner if stateful, migration, deterministic replay, performance budget, and rollback before implementation. Missing owners mean the feature remains an unresolved design question; no local mutable workaround is permitted.

### UI, accessibility, and acceptance

Show continuity tasks, willing participants, open questions, and contact limits in plain language. Avoid a “good survivor” label. The player can keep the board blank, decline to name a successor, or leave the meeting. Support accessible focus, text scaling, screen-reader description, controller back, reduced motion, and a visible private-conversation option. Load only the current shelter’s projection; do not rescan the campaign or all survivors. Review against existing succession, shelter, legacy, and ending plans before implementation. Acceptance requires a current-source premise audit, owner and consumer evidence, focused contract/data verification, save/replay coverage where relevant, accessibility review, and collision check against active plans. Treat every faction, location, and mechanic in this dossier as provisional until that review passes.
