The choice can preserve, delay, redirect, or refuse the request. Show the consequence before explanation. A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for endgame horizons and legacy frontiers. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. The packet may touch faction standing, route access, roster duty, shelter archive, relationship, expedition, or ending interpretation only through those authorities. It may not create a private truce score, route graph, calendar, inventory, reputation counter, or parallel legacy record.

#### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The mechanic should have a threshold, a visible cost, a reversible preparation state, and a deterministic result. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

At Slate Orchard Beacon, describe who built the room, which flood or fire altered it, who kept the key, and why one wall remains unpainted. Give the player a physical trace, a remembered phrase, a disputed interpretation, and a maintenance action. Returning to the site should show an object moved, repaired, withheld, or shared before any dialogue summarizes the change.

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Slate Orchard Beacon notices labor and weather. A representative of Red Lantern Horizon Authority speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to South Badger Assembly remembers a different sequence. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive a measurable roster, route, archive, or ending consequence.

#### Extended field 08 — Faction politics

The faction layer distinguishes Red Lantern Horizon Authority, South Badger Assembly, Slate Orchard Witnesses, and Cobalt Rain Custodians by resource, ritual, and risk rather than color. Red Lantern Horizon Authority wants a reliable public record, South Badger Assembly protects a route custom, Slate Orchard Witnesses values a scarce repair skill, and Cobalt Rain Custodians demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

#### Extended field 09 — Story and prose

The side quest opens with an ordinary sentence: someone asks whether the lamp, map, ledger, meal, or signal can wait one more night. The player’s answer changes who performs the task and what is remembered. Use restrained prose, concrete objects, and one silence that another character interprets differently. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants.

#### Extended field 10 — Late-game system

The late-game form is a major faction or frontier institution that can only appear after several owner-bound facts agree. It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

#### Extended field 11 — Data and catalog

Candidate content rows for temporary camp return charter carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Link every row to one canonical consumer and one command. Keep Cobalt Rain Frontier, South Badger Causeway, Slate Orchard Witnesses, and Cobalt Rain Custodians provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven.

#### Extended field 12 — Save and migration

Use the smallest existing save section. Capture the new fact, restore it, migrate older envelopes, tolerate an absent optional row, and make duplicate events idempotent. Define the pre-event, committed, refused, interrupted, and restored states. Do not encode prose branches in a panel cache. A rollback note must identify the event boundary and the owner responsible for undo or compensating projection.

#### Extended field 13 — Deterministic replay

Pin seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation. Avoid wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, hidden random choices, and locale-sensitive sorting. Include a late-arrival replay and a missing-record replay so optional content cannot alter the deterministic core unexpectedly.

#### Extended field 14 — UI and accessibility

The UI exposes a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard and controller back behavior, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, and confirmation for irreversible choices. Provide an audio or text alternative. If a record is missing, show a truthful unavailable state and preserve navigation. Archive and map panels consume projections; they do not own decisions.

#### Extended field 15 — Performance and lifecycle

Set budgets for catalog parse, query, event dispatch, archive projection, panel refresh, long text, and return visits. Load high-volume rows lazily, page them without changing order, dispose listeners on close, and avoid repeated full-catalog scans. Add one degradation path for a missing asset or provider. Note the smallest focused host smoke needed if the owner route is eventually implemented.

#### Extended field 16 — Acceptance and handoff

Acceptance requires premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable player command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and a rollback boundary. The handoff names untouched shared paths and labels this as design scaffolding. The final image is practical: a repaired latch, an amended map, a divided bowl, a chalk mark, a quiet signal, or a door left open by consent.

## Wave 55 extended depth receipt

The extended layer is documentation-only. Promotion requires current premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, reachable content, deterministic persistence and replay, accessibility, performance, and rollback evidence.


## Wave 55 capsule layer

These capsules extend the Wave 55 fields with additional playable scaffolds. Each remains provisional, owner-bound, and documentation-only.

### Wave 55 capsule 01: late notice witness at Red Lantern Horizon

**Opening and choice.** At **Red Lantern Horizon**, the player finds a practical problem that cannot be solved by rhetoric alone: a weather window is closing, a shared tool has two claimants, a missing person may be returning, a night signal is being misread, an apprentice is ready before the shelter is ready, a water ration has been counted twice, a quiet route carries an old debt, or a legacy object must be placed in another person’s hands. The player inspects the evidence, asks for consent, compares accounts, chooses a cost, defers, or leaves. The cost appears before commitment and a refusal keeps a safe return path.

**Authority and mechanic.** Route the action through the current owner for endgame horizons and legacy frontiers. Define one command, one event key, one resulting fact, one refusal result, one fallback, and one idempotency rule. A derived readiness view may combine existing standing, relationship, route, roster, shelter, archive, expedition, or ending facts, but it cannot become a second ledger or clock. The mechanic should make an ordinary task consequential: rescheduling a crossing changes who carries a tool, recording a signal changes which watch is asked to stand, or accepting a handover changes who is invited to the next meeting. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk version first.

**Place and shelter lore.** At **Slate Orchard Beacon**, describe the builder, the repair that saved the room, the person who still pays for that repair, and the mark that remains unexplained. At **Cobalt Rain Frontier**, place a contrasting trace: a patched hinge, a dry shelf, an erased route line, a bell rope, a teaching slate, or a bowl set aside. At **South Badger Causeway**, let a shelter custom make the history useful: a lamp is moved only after consent, a tool is returned sharpened, a guest cup is washed before dawn, or a route name is spoken once and then left unclaimed. Returning to the location shows a changed object before exposition.

**Characters and factions.** A resident speaks in concrete duties and notices who will carry the burden. A representative of **Red Lantern Horizon Authority** uses public language and wants an auditable result. A voice from **South Badger Assembly** protects a custom that looks inefficient until its history is heard. **Slate Orchard Witnesses** values a scarce skill, while **Cobalt Rain Custodians** asks who will witness the consequence after the player leaves. Give each voice a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and callback. The late-game factional version may convene a coalition, certify a passage, steward a shelter custom, or preserve a memory, but it may request and witness only through existing authorities.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

**Data and content volume.** Candidate rows carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Create arrival, inspection, task, hazard, rest, departure, return, calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, and late-arrival variants. Keep the names of **Red Lantern Horizon Authority**, **South Badger Assembly**, **Slate Orchard Witnesses**, and **Cobalt Rain Custodians** provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven. A missing optional row should collapse to a truthful unavailable state rather than alter the deterministic core.

**Persistence and replay.** Capture the smallest new fact through the existing save section. Define pre-action, committed, refused, interrupted, restored, migrated, and duplicate-event states. Pin the campaign seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation, including the late-arrival and missing-record cases. Do not use wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, locale-sensitive sorting, or hidden randomness in prose.

**UI, accessibility, and lifecycle.** Expose a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard/controller close and back, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, confirmation for irreversible actions, and text or audio alternatives. Panels consume owner projections and dispose listeners on close. High-volume rows load lazily and page without changing order. Set budgets for parse, query, dispatch, archive projection, refresh, and return visits; document the missing-provider path and the smallest eventual host smoke.

**Acceptance and handoff.** Accept the capsule only with premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and rollback. The handoff records untouched shared paths and labels the content as design scaffolding. The final image is small and physical: a cord retied, a cup passed over, a map corrected, a signal answered, a tool returned sharper, a meal divided, or a door left open because someone was asked first.

## Wave 55 late-game faction and playable arc dossier — The Reversible Camp Assembly

**Canon and collision status.** The Reversible Camp Assembly is proposed major late-game content, not a current catalog fact. Compare its role and all new names against current narrative data, active plans, system owners, save paths, and integration claims. If an equivalent authority already exists, fold the quests into it or retire the faction. All mechanics remain proposal-only.

### Mandate and opening incident at Third Signal

The Reversible Camp Assembly is a proposed major late-game frontier faction that treats first settlement as a trial with a planned dismantling or re-use path. It advocates small reversible structures, clear material ownership, and an agreed return point if the trial fails. It differs from the Hearthline Assembly’s shelter continuity: its subject is a temporary frontier site and what happens to that site when its purpose changes. It owns no camp simulation, construction inventory, or ending state. At Third Signal, the first canvas shelter has been assembled beside a new route marker. Half the group wants to move in before the weather turns; the other half says no one has written down how the frame will be dismantled or where its pieces will go. The player can propose a limited occupancy trial, complete a return plan, ask the group to wait, or decide that the location is not ready.

### Five-quest playable spine

Quest 1 — The Tent with No Owner: establish who brought each component using current inventory and expedition records; do not infer ownership from who assembled it. Quest 2 — One Night at North Bench Settlement: host a limited stay and collect practical feedback without claiming permanent settlement. Quest 3 — The Frame on Pale Ridge Road: inspect whether a structure blocks an existing passage or can be reused at another location. Quest 4 — The Dismantling Practice: let a crew rehearse packing the shelter, document one unsafe step, and revise the instruction. Quest 5 — The Trial Charter: convene the Assembly at Homeward Switch to choose continue, pause, dismantle, or transfer materials through current owners. Callback shows an occupied tent, a returned frame, or a marked site awaiting another decision.

### Internal divisions and late-game faction role

The Stay-and-Test group wants evidence from occupancy; the Pack-It-Back crew insists the return plan be complete before assembly; the Local Builders want any construction to benefit the neighboring shelter; the Path Stewards object if temporary structures block travel. Their conflicts make a late-game organization rather than a mere construction menu. Membership is voluntary, and no one is ordered to remain at the site. The faction acts by convening affected people and requesting supported actions. It cannot impose its rule beyond the participants who accept it. Its late-game scale comes from linked quests and authored callbacks, not an independent territory, resource ledger, relationship score, route graph, or ending resolver.

### Character personalities and relationship beats

Kiva Renn is good at building and uncomfortable with dismantling what she made. Oren Vos can pack a frame quickly but refuses to be the only person who knows how. Sella Marr lives near the trial site and worries that “temporary” will become permanent without asking her. Pavi Noll wants to join the expedition but asks whether they can leave after one night without being called a failure. Their dialogue must preserve reversibility in emotional as well as physical terms. Distinct voices should persist across branches; no character becomes a one-line advocate for the player’s preferred choice. Relationship changes, if any, go through the existing relationship owner. Include a minor character’s refusal or correction as a meaningful outcome.

### Prose and quest variants

Prose fragments: “The tent stood. The plan for taking it down did not.” “Oren put the last peg beside the first and waited.” “Sella asked whether the trail would still belong to the people who used it yesterday.” Include continue, limited trial, pause, dismantle, transfer, and site-abandonment versions. The player should revisit after a weather turn and see use or absence. Epilogue language reflects actual campaign and expedition facts, not a separate settlement score. Each quest needs an entry condition, owner-routed action, cost preview, refusal, recovery, missing-data fallback, and late callback. Make the mechanic visible through a task or changed object. Preserve a scene where the player leaves without resolving the dispute.

### Proposed feature or system seam

The proposed “reversible camp” feature composes existing colony, expedition, vehicle, inventory, route, shelter, and campaign owners. It must not add a second build inventory or site registry. Structure rows reference an existing location and candidate construction data only if current schema and consumers support them. Dismantling and transfer use current inventory and colony commands; absent support keeps the activity narrative-only. Stateful outcomes use current save sections, deterministic IDs, migration-safe defaults, paired replay, and a rollback path that returns or leaves items only through existing owners. This proposal introduces authored data and behavior over existing authorities unless a future architecture decision explicitly creates a new owner. Name producer, consumer, host route, event contract, save/migration path when stateful, deterministic replay, focused verification, performance budget, and rollback before implementation. A missing premise remains a design blocker; do not fill it with local mutable state.

### UI, accessibility, and acceptance

The frontier panel shows trial duration only when an existing campaign owner exposes it, structure components, current owner, path impact, dismantle steps, and return choices. It distinguishes temporary from permanent by authored state and never assumes a timer. Support keyboard/controller action order, scaling, map labels, readable assembly instructions, and a no-audio alternative. Lazy-load one site’s rows and invalidate on relevant owner events. Test old-save fallback and prove the ending resolver remains unchanged when optional camp data is absent. Candidate content is ready for implementation review only after current evidence proves its owner and reachable consumer, plus a collision check against active plans. Include keyboard/controller behavior, accessible information alternatives, bounded catalog access, safe missing-content behavior, and an honest non-implementation status.

The packet is not an implementation claim; it is ready only for a safe-slice review.


## Wave 56 supplemental receipt

The supplemental packets preserve the active twenty-field structure and broaden the playable content bank. They remain provisional until current catalog, ownership, save, replay, UI, accessibility, performance, and rollback evidence is attached.


## Wave 56 extended depth layer

This larger tranche adds six extended packets per plan. They deepen the active twenty fields while keeping all mechanics, catalog rows, factions, locations, shelter customs, and late-game institutions provisional and owner-bound.

### Wave 56 extended depth packet 01: copper braid listening table at Red Lantern Horizon

#### Extended field 01 — Premise and canon

The copper braid listening table begins as a premise audit around Red Lantern Horizon. The player is asked to count the lamps before opening the door, but the proposal remains provisional until current source, JSON authority, event producer, host consumer, and ownership ledger are cited. Record the nearest existing seam, the exact absent seam, and the collision to exclude. If the premise is already represented, fold the prose into that owner and retire this packet rather than creating a duplicate.

#### Extended field 02 — Player loop

The loop has six readable beats: arrive at Red Lantern Horizon, inspect a practical sign, hear a resident’s account, choose a cost, perform one visible task, and return after the next weather or duty turn. The choice can preserve, delay, redirect, or refuse the request. Show the consequence before explanation. A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for endgame horizons and legacy frontiers. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. The packet may touch faction standing, route access, roster duty, shelter archive, relationship, expedition, or ending interpretation only through those authorities. It may not create a private truce score, route graph, calendar, inventory, reputation counter, or parallel legacy record.

#### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The mechanic should have a threshold, a visible cost, a reversible preparation state, and a deterministic result. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

At Slate Orchard Beacon, describe who built the room, which flood or fire altered it, who kept the key, and why one wall remains unpainted. Give the player a physical trace, a remembered phrase, a disputed interpretation, and a maintenance action. Returning to the site should show an object moved, repaired, withheld, or shared before any dialogue summarizes the change.

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Slate Orchard Beacon notices labor and weather. A representative of Red Lantern Horizon Authority speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to South Badger Assembly remembers a different sequence. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive a measurable roster, route, archive, or ending consequence.

#### Extended field 08 — Faction politics

The faction layer distinguishes Red Lantern Horizon Authority, South Badger Assembly, Slate Orchard Witnesses, and Cobalt Rain Custodians by resource, ritual, and risk rather than color. Red Lantern Horizon Authority wants a reliable public record, South Badger Assembly protects a route custom, Slate Orchard Witnesses values a scarce repair skill, and Cobalt Rain Custodians demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

#### Extended field 09 — Story and prose

The side quest opens with an ordinary sentence: someone asks whether the lamp, map, ledger, meal, or signal can wait one more night. The player’s answer changes who performs the task and what is remembered. Use restrained prose, concrete objects, and one silence that another character interprets differently. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants.

#### Extended field 10 — Late-game system

The late-game form is a major faction or frontier institution that can only appear after several owner-bound facts agree. It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

#### Extended field 11 — Data and catalog

Candidate content rows for copper braid listening table carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Link every row to one canonical consumer and one command. Keep Cobalt Rain Frontier, South Badger Causeway, Slate Orchard Witnesses, and Cobalt Rain Custodians provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven.

#### Extended field 12 — Save and migration

Use the smallest existing save section. Capture the new fact, restore it, migrate older envelopes, tolerate an absent optional row, and make duplicate events idempotent. Define the pre-event, committed, refused, interrupted, and restored states. Do not encode prose branches in a panel cache. A rollback note must identify the event boundary and the owner responsible for undo or compensating projection.

#### Extended field 13 — Deterministic replay

Pin seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation. Avoid wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, hidden random choices, and locale-sensitive sorting. Include a late-arrival replay and a missing-record replay so optional content cannot alter the deterministic core unexpectedly.

#### Extended field 14 — UI and accessibility

The UI exposes a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard and controller back behavior, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, and confirmation for irreversible choices. Provide an audio or text alternative. If a record is missing, show a truthful unavailable state and preserve navigation. Archive and map panels consume projections; they do not own decisions.

#### Extended field 15 — Performance and lifecycle

Set budgets for catalog parse, query, event dispatch, archive projection, panel refresh, long text, and return visits. Load high-volume rows lazily, page them without changing order, dispose listeners on close, and avoid repeated full-catalog scans. Add one degradation path for a missing asset or provider. Note the smallest focused host smoke needed if the owner route is eventually implemented.

#### Extended field 16 — Acceptance and handoff

Acceptance requires premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable player command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and a rollback boundary. The handoff names untouched shared paths and labels this as design scaffolding. The final image is practical: a repaired latch, an amended map, a divided bowl, a chalk mark, a quiet signal, or a door left open by consent.

### Wave 56 extended depth packet 06: far porch invitation charter at Red Lantern Horizon

#### Extended field 01 — Premise and canon

The far porch invitation charter begins as a premise audit around Red Lantern Horizon. The player is asked to return with a corrected map, but the proposal remains provisional until current source, JSON authority, event producer, host consumer, and ownership ledger are cited. Record the nearest existing seam, the exact absent seam, and the collision to exclude. If the premise is already represented, fold the prose into that owner and retire this packet rather than creating a duplicate.

#### Extended field 02 — Player loop

The loop has six readable beats: arrive at Red Lantern Horizon, inspect a practical sign, hear a resident’s account, choose a cost, perform one visible task, and return after the next weather or duty turn. The choice can preserve, delay, redirect, or refuse the request. Show the consequence before explanation. A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for endgame horizons and legacy frontiers. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. The packet may touch faction standing, route access, roster duty, shelter archive, relationship, expedition, or ending interpretation only through those authorities. It may not create a private truce score, route graph, calendar, inventory, reputation counter, or parallel legacy record.

#### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The mechanic should have a threshold, a visible cost, a reversible preparation state, and a deterministic result. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

At Slate Orchard Beacon, describe who built the room, which flood or fire altered it, who kept the key, and why one wall remains unpainted. Give the player a physical trace, a remembered phrase, a disputed interpretation, and a maintenance action. Returning to the site should show an object moved, repaired, withheld, or shared before any dialogue summarizes the change.

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Slate Orchard Beacon notices labor and weather. A representative of Red Lantern Horizon Authority speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to South Badger Assembly remembers a different sequence. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive a measurable roster, route, archive, or ending consequence.

Red Lantern Horizon Authority wants a reliable public record, South Badger Assembly protects a route custom, Slate Orchard Witnesses values a scarce repair skill, and Cobalt Rain Custodians demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

### Wave 56 capsule 01: quiet witness timing at Red Lantern Horizon

**Opening and choice.** At **Red Lantern Horizon**, the player finds a practical problem that cannot be solved by rhetoric alone: a weather window is closing, a shared tool has two claimants, a missing person may be returning, a night signal is being misread, an apprentice is ready before the shelter is ready, a water ration has been counted twice, a quiet route carries an old debt, or a legacy object must be placed in another person’s hands. The player inspects the evidence, asks for consent, compares accounts, chooses a cost, defers, or leaves. The cost appears before commitment and a refusal keeps a safe return path.

**Authority and mechanic.** Route the action through the current owner for endgame horizons and legacy frontiers. Define one command, one event key, one resulting fact, one refusal result, one fallback, and one idempotency rule. A derived readiness view may combine existing standing, relationship, route, roster, shelter, archive, expedition, or ending facts, but it cannot become a second ledger or clock. The mechanic should make an ordinary task consequential: rescheduling a crossing changes who carries a tool, recording a signal changes which watch is asked to stand, or accepting a handover changes who is invited to the next meeting. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk version first.

**Place and shelter lore.** At **Slate Orchard Beacon**, describe the builder, the repair that saved the room, the person who still pays for that repair, and the mark that remains unexplained. At **Cobalt Rain Frontier**, place a contrasting trace: a patched hinge, a dry shelf, an erased route line, a bell rope, a teaching slate, or a bowl set aside. At **South Badger Causeway**, let a shelter custom make the history useful: a lamp is moved only after consent, a tool is returned sharpened, a guest cup is washed before dawn, or a route name is spoken once and then left unclaimed. Returning to the location shows a changed object before exposition.

**Characters and factions.** A resident speaks in concrete duties and notices who will carry the burden. A representative of **Red Lantern Horizon Authority** uses public language and wants an auditable result. A voice from **South Badger Assembly** protects a custom that looks inefficient until its history is heard. **Slate Orchard Witnesses** values a scarce skill, while **Cobalt Rain Custodians** asks who will witness the consequence after the player leaves. Give each voice a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and callback. The late-game factional version may convene a coalition, certify a passage, steward a shelter custom, or preserve a memory, but it may request and witness only through existing authorities.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

**Data and content volume.** Candidate rows carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Create arrival, inspection, task, hazard, rest, departure, return, calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, and late-arrival variants. Keep the names of **Red Lantern Horizon Authority**, **South Badger Assembly**, **Slate Orchard Witnesses**, and **Cobalt Rain Custodians** provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven. A missing optional row should collapse to a truthful unavailable state rather than alter the deterministic core.

**Persistence and replay.** Capture the smallest new fact through the existing save section. Define pre-action, committed, refused, interrupted, restored, migrated, and duplicate-event states. Pin the campaign seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation, including the late-arrival and missing-record cases. Do not use wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, locale-sensitive sorting, or hidden randomness in prose.

**UI, accessibility, and lifecycle.** Expose a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard/controller close and back, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, confirmation for irreversible actions, and text or audio alternatives. Panels consume owner projections and dispose listeners on close. High-volume rows load lazily and page without changing order. Set budgets for parse, query, dispatch, archive projection, refresh, and return visits; document the missing-provider path and the smallest eventual host smoke.

**Acceptance and handoff.** Accept the capsule only with premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and rollback. The handoff records untouched shared paths and labels the content as design scaffolding. The final image is small and physical: a cord retied, a cup passed over, a map corrected, a signal answered, a tool returned sharper, a meal divided, or a door left open because someone was asked first.

## Wave 56 extended playable-content volume — endgame horizons and legacy frontiers

This volume adds a second authored layer for the current twenty fields. It supplies detailed scenario records, location traces, character voices, high-volume candidate rows, system sketches, and playable acceptance cases. Every named faction and location is provisional; content must merge with a current owner or stop if the premise already exists. No new mutable authority is implied.

### Wave 56 design module 01: Consent-first invitation

**Player-facing behavior.** In Northern Beacon, the player approaches Field Rest Camp with one concrete need. The interface names the person affected, the practical task, the cost of acting now, and the safe alternatives. An invitation can be carried, posted, or withheld. The player sees who can read each form before choosing; no invitation itself grants standing. A preview does not promise the outcome; it distinguishes known facts from requests and unresolved information.

**System boundary.** Define the producer, current authority, event or command, consumer, refusal result, missing-data fallback, and idempotency rule. If the feature touches Northern Beacon Choir, its representative may request an action but cannot mutate an owner’s state. One observable world response—an adjusted notice, a room prepared, a task handed over, or a route marked uncertain—proves that the content is reachable.

**Quality case.** Include a focused contract check, a stable event key, a save round trip only for owner-supported state, and paired replay with fixed inputs. Test late arrival and absent content. Performance work should bound lookup to referenced IDs and dispose UI listeners when the scene closes. Acceptance stops when the current owner or host route cannot be named.

### Wave 56 location and shelter lore card 01: who built the room

Use **Northern Beacon** to tell the history through an actionable detail. The player discovers who built or repaired the place, what changed after that work, and who still maintains it. Give the location one sensory signature that does not depend on color alone, one object that can be inspected, one account that may be disputed, and one safe way to leave. Shelter customs must have a practical use and a person who can revise them. Keep the prose restrained: describe the smell of wet canvas, a chipped cup, chalk beneath a ledge, or a latch polished by many hands. Return visits show a physical change before a lore summary. Do not turn a memorial, injury, or private room into a collectible reward.

A refusal is phrased clearly and does not imply later punishment unless a supported system fact produces it.

**Variant keys.** Provide calm, under-pressure, tired, recently helped, previously refused, late-arrival, and no-record variants. Keep the factual content consistent across localized and audio versions. A voice callback should change only when its event prerequisite is true. Review for repetitive metaphors, unearned intimacy, and dialogue that makes the player the only person able to solve a shelter problem.

## Wave 56 extended-volume receipt

This volume provides additional implementation-ready planning material without promoting provisional content to canon. Before any implementation, re-run the premise audit, claim exact paths, identify one existing authority per concern, and verify focused save, replay, UI, accessibility, and performance requirements. The additions do not authorize new mutable state or production code.


## Wave 56 late-game faction dossier — The Far Porch Compact

### Premise and place in the campaign
The Far Porch Compact is a proposed late-game relationship among remote shelters that want contact and mutual warning without joining a central authority. Its members live beyond the Northern Beacon's dependable signal and have learned to distrust promises that arrive without a named sender or return route. The Compact's first principle is modest: an invitation is not a treaty; a warning is not a demand; a delayed answer is not a refusal. This gives the endgame a quieter form of convergence, in which distant groups can recognize one another while retaining local choices.

The faction begins when the Field Rest Camp receives a reply to a message nobody there remembers sending. The mark is genuine but the route is uncertain. The player must discover whether a displaced group copied a beacon pattern, reused an old tag, or independently chose the same signal. The story should make evidence and uncertainty playable without turning communications into a new universal radio authority. Any implemented message flow must use the current communications, quest, and campaign-state owners.

### Five-quest arc
1. **A Light beyond the Rise.** A distant signal appears at Long Rise Trail. The player records its timing and context using existing journal and observation mechanisms, then waits for a repeat rather than assuming intent.
2. **The Sender Who Wasn't Named.** Search a damaged handoff point and find several plausible senders. Each has a credible reason to use the beacon. The player can ask, observe, or leave a noncommittal acknowledgment.
3. **A Reply with Room in It.** Draft a short answer that includes a return method, uncertainty, and a limit on what the shelter can promise. Dialogue choices should distinguish invitation, aid offer, warning, and alliance.
4. **The Beacon Goes Dark.** Weather interrupts contact during a fragile local situation. The player must choose whether to protect the beacon, deliver a physical message, or postpone contact. No choice should imply that remote residents are disposable scenery.
5. **Porches Facing Outward.** At Return Mark Shelter, the groups decide on a seasonal check-in, a pair of named contacts, or an open invitation with no scheduled obligation. The closing scene shows a real consequence: a voice, a repaired signal, a shared warning, or a respectfully unanswered call.

### People, voice, and internal tension
Ari Voss, keeper of the Northern Beacon, marks each transmission with weather and confidence because a false alarm once emptied a shelter. Pell Sorn, a traveler at Field Rest Camp, wants contact to remain human and refuses to speak for people who are absent. Lio Fen, a young listener, worries that careful procedure will become an excuse never to answer. The **Signal Stewards** favor verified repetition, the **Porch Listeners** value open contact, and the **Unsent Letter Circle** protects the right to remain unreachable. Their views shape available scenes but do not create a second campaign relationship system.

### Feature and implementation contract
The proposed feature is a small set of message-intent labels and visible delivery uncertainty, expressed through existing quest dialogue, radio content, journal, and campaign flags where supported. A signal can be heard, attributed, acknowledged, or answered; these states must not collapse into “faction joined.” Do not add an independent radio network or global settlement graph. Communication timing and asset playback remain with existing owners. Late-game records must survive saves through the current campaign persistence path if they affect future scenes. A missing persistence owner blocks mechanics but not the content arc.

### Content and validation slices
Candidate material includes five quests, four beacon scenes, six signal records, eight dialogue fragments, four location entries, and three ending variants. Use Northern Beacon, Field Rest Camp, Long Rise Trail, and Return Mark Shelter as candidate locations. Review all signals for plausible source, range, weather context, and return route. Check narrative continuity against existing radio/quest flags, verify data references, and test message delivery in the real UI at the target resolution. If any new campaign state is proposed, map it to the existing owner and prove capture/restore and deterministic replay before claiming implementation. Avoid time-based random signal generation.

### Sample scene
Ari waits through three full sweeps before answering. Lio watches the dark ridge. “Maybe they think we ignored them.” Ari points to the weather strip pinned beside the lamp. “They can see the same storm.” Pell writes a reply that begins **We heard you** and ends **we cannot promise a road tonight**. Lio asks whether that is enough. No one answers for the people on the other side of the rise.

### Acceptance and rollback
Accept the design when signals communicate uncertainty, every contact choice preserves the sender's autonomy, and any persistent result uses current campaign ownership. Roll back mechanics that imply instant reliable communication, create an unowned faction score, or auto-enlist remote shelters. Keep the story complete as a sequence of authored encounters if the live game lacks a compatible message system.

### Pass 615: Custody of the Last Span

This pass extends endgame stewardship succession and site handback with custody of the last span. It is a proposal over the current authority owned by the existing ending resolver, campaign legacy, campaign, faction, expedition, shelter/colony, and archive authorities identified by a fresh premise audit; no parallel ending record is presumed. The named factions and places are provisional labels, not catalog facts. Start with a source, data, consumer, and ownership audit; if an existing record already expresses the idea, fold this material into that record or stop. The player should make a legible choice that affects a practical task, a remembered relationship, a route, or a late-game interpretation.

#### 1. Premise evidence

## Wave 57 supplemental receipt

The supplemental packets preserve the active twenty-field structure and broaden the playable content bank. They remain provisional until current catalog, ownership, save, replay, UI, accessibility, performance, and rollback evidence is attached.


## Wave 57 extended depth layer

This larger tranche adds six extended packets per plan. They deepen the active twenty fields while keeping all mechanics, catalog rows, factions, locations, shelter customs, and late-game institutions provisional and owner-bound.

### Wave 57 extended depth packet 01: repair-credit hearing at Farrier’s Last Bridge

#### Extended field 01 — Premise and canon

The repair-credit hearing begins as a premise audit around Farrier’s Last Bridge. The player is asked to read the repair record before hearing the apology, but the proposal remains provisional until current source, JSON authority, event producer, host consumer, and ownership ledger are cited. Record the nearest existing seam, the exact absent seam, and the collision to exclude. If the premise is already represented, fold the prose into that owner and retire this packet rather than creating a duplicate.

#### Extended field 02 — Player loop

The loop has six readable beats: arrive at Farrier’s Last Bridge, inspect a practical sign, hear a resident’s account, choose a cost, perform one visible task, and return after the next weather or duty turn. The choice can preserve, delay, redirect, or refuse the request. Show the consequence before explanation. A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for endgame stewardship succession and site handback. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. The packet may touch faction standing, route access, roster duty, shelter archive, relationship, expedition, or ending interpretation only through those authorities. It may not create a private truce score, route graph, calendar, inventory, reputation counter, or parallel legacy record.

#### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The mechanic should have a threshold, a visible cost, a reversible preparation state, and a deterministic result. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

At Hollow Way Nursery, describe who built the room, which flood or fire altered it, who kept the key, and why one wall remains unpainted. Give the player a physical trace, a remembered phrase, a disputed interpretation, and a maintenance action. Returning to the site should show an object moved, repaired, withheld, or shared before any dialogue summarizes the change.

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Hollow Way Nursery notices labor and weather. A representative of Continuance Assembly speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to Handover Stewards remembers a different sequence. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive a measurable roster, route, archive, or ending consequence.

#### Extended field 08 — Faction politics

The faction layer distinguishes Continuance Assembly, Handover Stewards, Open Horizon Custodians, and Return Route Advocates by resource, ritual, and risk rather than color. Continuance Assembly wants a reliable public record, Handover Stewards protects a route custom, Open Horizon Custodians values a scarce repair skill, and Return Route Advocates demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

#### Extended field 09 — Story and prose

The side quest opens with an ordinary sentence: someone asks whether the lamp, map, ledger, meal, or signal can wait one more night. The player’s answer changes who performs the task and what is remembered. Use restrained prose, concrete objects, and one silence that another character interprets differently. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants.

#### Extended field 10 — Late-game system

The late-game form is a major faction or frontier institution that can only appear after several owner-bound facts agree. It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

#### Extended field 11 — Data and catalog

Candidate content rows for repair-credit hearing carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Link every row to one canonical consumer and one command. Keep Low Signal Roof, Turnback Granary, Open Horizon Custodians, and Return Route Advocates provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven.

#### Extended field 12 — Save and migration

Use the smallest existing save section. Capture the new fact, restore it, migrate older envelopes, tolerate an absent optional row, and make duplicate events idempotent. Define the pre-event, committed, refused, interrupted, and restored states. Do not encode prose branches in a panel cache. A rollback note must identify the event boundary and the owner responsible for undo or compensating projection.

#### Extended field 13 — Deterministic replay

Pin seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation. Avoid wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, hidden random choices, and locale-sensitive sorting. Include a late-arrival replay and a missing-record replay so optional content cannot alter the deterministic core unexpectedly.

#### Extended field 14 — UI and accessibility

The UI exposes a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard and controller back behavior, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, and confirmation for irreversible choices. Provide an audio or text alternative. If a record is missing, show a truthful unavailable state and preserve navigation. Archive and map panels consume projections; they do not own decisions.

#### Extended field 15 — Performance and lifecycle

Set budgets for catalog parse, query, event dispatch, archive projection, panel refresh, long text, and return visits. Load high-volume rows lazily, page them without changing order, dispose listeners on close, and avoid repeated full-catalog scans. Add one degradation path for a missing asset or provider. Note the smallest focused host smoke needed if the owner route is eventually implemented.

#### Extended field 16 — Acceptance and handoff

Acceptance requires premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable player command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and a rollback boundary. The handoff names untouched shared paths and labels this as design scaffolding. The final image is practical: a repaired latch, an amended map, a divided bowl, a chalk mark, a quiet signal, or a door left open by consent.

A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for endgame stewardship succession and site handback. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. #### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

The faction layer distinguishes Continuance Assembly, Handover Stewards, Open Horizon Custodians, and Return Route Advocates by resource, ritual, and risk rather than color. Continuance Assembly wants a reliable public record, Handover Stewards protects a route custom, Open Horizon Custodians values a scarce repair skill, and Return Route Advocates demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

The side quest opens with an ordinary sentence: someone asks whether the lamp, map, ledger, meal, or signal can wait one more night. It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

### Wave 57 capsule 01: repair hours disclosed at Farrier’s Last Bridge

**Opening and choice.** At **Farrier’s Last Bridge**, the player finds a practical problem that cannot be solved by rhetoric alone: a weather window is closing, a shared tool has two claimants, a missing person may be returning, a night signal is being misread, an apprentice is ready before the shelter is ready, a water ration has been counted twice, a quiet route carries an old debt, or a legacy object must be placed in another person’s hands. The player inspects the evidence, asks for consent, compares accounts, chooses a cost, defers, or leaves. The cost appears before commitment and a refusal keeps a safe return path.

**Authority and mechanic.** Route the action through the current owner for endgame stewardship succession and site handback. Define one command, one event key, one resulting fact, one refusal result, one fallback, and one idempotency rule. A derived readiness view may combine existing standing, relationship, route, roster, shelter, archive, expedition, or ending facts, but it cannot become a second ledger or clock. The mechanic should make an ordinary task consequential: rescheduling a crossing changes who carries a tool, recording a signal changes which watch is asked to stand, or accepting a handover changes who is invited to the next meeting. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk version first.

**Place and shelter lore.** At **Hollow Way Nursery**, describe the builder, the repair that saved the room, the person who still pays for that repair, and the mark that remains unexplained. At **Low Signal Roof**, place a contrasting trace: a patched hinge, a dry shelf, an erased route line, a bell rope, a teaching slate, or a bowl set aside. At **Turnback Granary**, let a shelter custom make the history useful: a lamp is moved only after consent, a tool is returned sharpened, a guest cup is washed before dawn, or a route name is spoken once and then left unclaimed. Returning to the location shows a changed object before exposition.

**Characters and factions.** A resident speaks in concrete duties and notices who will carry the burden. A representative of **Continuance Assembly** uses public language and wants an auditable result. A voice from **Handover Stewards** protects a custom that looks inefficient until its history is heard. **Open Horizon Custodians** values a scarce skill, while **Return Route Advocates** asks who will witness the consequence after the player leaves. Give each voice a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and callback. The late-game factional version may convene a coalition, certify a passage, steward a shelter custom, or preserve a memory, but it may request and witness only through existing authorities.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

**Data and content volume.** Candidate rows carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Create arrival, inspection, task, hazard, rest, departure, return, calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, and late-arrival variants. Keep the names of **Continuance Assembly**, **Handover Stewards**, **Open Horizon Custodians**, and **Return Route Advocates** provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven. A missing optional row should collapse to a truthful unavailable state rather than alter the deterministic core.

**Persistence and replay.** Capture the smallest new fact through the existing save section. Define pre-action, committed, refused, interrupted, restored, migrated, and duplicate-event states. Pin the campaign seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation, including the late-arrival and missing-record cases. Do not use wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, locale-sensitive sorting, or hidden randomness in prose.

**UI, accessibility, and lifecycle.** Expose a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard/controller close and back, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, confirmation for irreversible actions, and text or audio alternatives. Panels consume owner projections and dispose listeners on close. High-volume rows load lazily and page without changing order. Set budgets for parse, query, dispatch, archive projection, refresh, and return visits; document the missing-provider path and the smallest eventual host smoke.

**Acceptance and handoff.** Accept the capsule only with premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and rollback. The handoff records untouched shared paths and labels the content as design scaffolding. The final image is small and physical: a cord retied, a cup passed over, a map corrected, a signal answered, a tool returned sharper, a meal divided, or a door left open because someone was asked first.

The player inspects the evidence, asks for consent, compares accounts, chooses a cost, defers, or leaves. The cost appears before commitment and a refusal keeps a safe return path.

**Authority and mechanic.** Route the action through the current owner for endgame stewardship succession and site handback. Define one command, one event key, one resulting fact, one refusal result, one fallback, and one idempotency rule. A derived readiness view may combine existing standing, relationship, route, roster, shelter, archive, expedition, or ending facts, but it cannot become a second ledger or clock. The mechanic should make an ordinary task consequential: rescheduling a crossing changes who carries a tool, recording a signal changes which watch is asked to stand, or accepting a handover changes who is invited to the next meeting. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk version first.

**Place and shelter lore.** At **Hollow Way Nursery**, describe the builder, the repair that saved the room, the person who still pays for that repair, and the mark that remains unexplained. At **Low Signal Roof**, place a contrasting trace: a patched hinge, a dry shelf, an erased route line, a bell rope, a teaching slate, or a bowl set aside. At **Turnback Granary**, let a shelter custom make the history useful: a lamp is moved only after consent, a tool is returned sharpened, a guest cup is washed before dawn, or a route name is spoken once and then left unclaimed. Returning to the location shows a changed object before exposition.

**Characters and factions.** A resident speaks in concrete duties and notices who will carry the burden. A representative of **Continuance Assembly** uses public language and wants an auditable result. A voice from **Handover Stewards** protects a custom that looks inefficient until its history is heard. **Open Horizon Custodians** values a scarce skill, while **Return Route Advocates** asks who will witness the consequence after the player leaves. Give each voice a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and callback. The late-game factional version may convene a coalition, certify a passage, steward a shelter custom, or preserve a memory, but it may request and witness only through existing authorities.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

**Data and content volume.** Candidate rows carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Create arrival, inspection, task, hazard, rest, departure, return, calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, and late-arrival variants. Keep the names of **Continuance Assembly**, **Handover Stewards**, **Open Horizon Custodians**, and **Return Route Advocates** provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven. A missing optional row should collapse to a truthful unavailable state rather than alter the deterministic core.

**Persistence and replay.** Capture the smallest new fact through the existing save section. Define pre-action, committed, refused, interrupted, restored, migrated, and duplicate-event states. Pin the campaign seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation, including the late-arrival and missing-record cases. Do not use wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, locale-sensitive sorting, or hidden randomness in prose.

**UI, accessibility, and lifecycle.** Expose a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard/controller close and back, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, confirmation for irreversible actions, and text or audio alternatives. Panels consume owner projections and dispose listeners on close. High-volume rows load lazily and page without changing order. Set budgets for parse, query, dispatch, archive projection, refresh, and return visits; document the missing-provider path and the smallest eventual host smoke.

**Acceptance and handoff.** Accept the capsule only with premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and rollback. The handoff records untouched shared paths and labels the content as design scaffolding. The final image is small and physical: a cord retied, a cup passed over, a map corrected, a signal answered, a tool returned sharper, a meal divided, or a door left open because someone was asked first.

## Wave 57 capsule receipt

The capsule layer remains documentation-only and is ready for premise review, not production promotion.


## Wave 57 playable-content atlas — endgame stewardship succession and site handback

This atlas deepens the active twenty-field plan with a new integrated story and mechanics layer. Candidate places, names, systems, and factions are provisional. The separate prose-first Wave 57 plans were indexed but not copied; this wave avoids their six anchor locations. Every stateful proposal below must map to a current owner before implementation.

### Narrative throughline and campaign rhythm

The campaign runs through four movements. At Farrier’s Last Bridge, the player first sees a practical discrepancy rather than a faction banner. At Hollow Way Nursery, a person explains the cost of leaving it unresolved. At Low Signal Roof, the player tests one response under low pressure. At Turnback Granary, a broader group tries to make that response repeatable and discovers what the first solution failed to address. The final movement returns to the opening object after other residents have had time to act. This rhythm keeps story, task, and consequence joined: a record changes hands, a cup is retested, a task is declined, or a key waits for an accepting custodian.

A major story decision cannot be solved by a single persuasion check. The player may learn, defer, offer help, revise the proposal, leave, or refuse. Each route needs a readable immediate cost and a later callback. Keep emotional resolution separate from mechanical completion: a repaired room does not force forgiveness; a safe water notice does not prove the source permanently safe; a successful trial task does not assign a new job; and a site handoff does not guarantee that the receiving group will continue the same custom.

#### Mechanic 01: site handback proposal with explicit receiver acceptance

**Player-facing loop.** At Farrier’s Last Bridge, Dema Quill presents one situation that can be understood by inspection before the player commits. The available responses are to check the evidence, ask the affected person, compare an alternative, perform the bounded task, wait for another party, or decline. The feature should reveal the cost in ordinary terms: time from a shift, a route detour, a limited number of supplies, a public disclosure, or a duty that needs a named replacement. The player must be able to back out before the irreversible step.

**Rule and owner boundary.** The candidate rule is: record only the observable fact that the existing Handover Stewards quest or current domain owner can support; derive any display from that fact; and never infer consent, safety, reconciliation, assignment, or successful stewardship from silence. No parallel counter, schedule, route graph, water store, biography, claim ledger, or ending resolver is authorized. ### Story and side-quest production cards

#### Quest 01: Custody of the Last Span

**Opening image.** At Farrier’s Last Bridge, Fen Tav finds a physical sign that the previous account is incomplete. The sign is useful but not definitive: a corrected receipt, a changed water mark, a blank role line, or a key returned without a receiver. The first dialogue invites observation and does not presume the player knows which group is right. Handover Stewards has a practical stake, while another resident bears a different cost.

**Playable sequence.** The player examines the trace, asks one witness a specific question, and performs or declines one bounded action. Offer three authored paths: act now with a known cost, wait for more evidence while accepting delay, or leave the matter unresolved. A failed attempt reveals a new fact or enables recovery. A successful task changes a physical condition or a supported owner projection, then gives the affected person a chance to comment without requiring gratitude.

**Branch and return.** Include a direct refusal branch, a partial-completion branch, and a late-arrival variant. Record no more than the current quest or campaign owner supports. On return, change a prop before the summary: a name is corrected, a sample seal is replaced, an inspection mark is dated, or a key is left on the public hook. The journal line names the result and its limits. A missing optional row must not block travel, shelter use, or later story.

### Character personality and relationship mini-arcs

#### Character arc 01: Dema Quill

**Established posture.** Dema Quill is a handover steward who trusts a task list more than a farewell speech. Show this through a repeated action, not a biography panel: checking a seam, turning a sample strip toward the light, rewriting a public line, pausing before a task, or counting who returned. Their immediate want is to complete one practical responsibility without having someone else define what it means. Their fear is specific to this story and should be stated only when trust and timing make it credible.

**Three playable beats.** First, the player witnesses the character’s skill or boundary at Farrier’s Last Bridge. Second, a pressure event lets the player ask, offer help, or step back; the character can decline without a hidden penalty. Third, a return scene shows the character correcting the player’s assumption or changing their own plan. Handover Stewards may pressure or support the choice, but it cannot speak for the character. The ending uses existing relationship or quest state only if that owner supports it. Include one line of humor, one line under pressure, one apology, and one boundary statement.

### Return-visit and prose variants

#### Return variant 01: Farrier’s Last Bridge

On a calm return, Mira Selt changes one ordinary object and offers a short update. Under pressure, the same character states the immediate limit first. After refusal, they acknowledge that the player left the choice with them. After a failed task, they reveal one new clue or a safe next step. On late arrival, the person who acted explains what they did before the player arrived; the player is not credited for it. If the relevant record is missing, the scene says the history is unavailable and continues. Keep the callback under a few sentences, use the same underlying facts across audio and text, and avoid turning hardship into a reward.

## Wave 57 late-game major faction dossier — The Continuance Assembly

The Continuance Assembly is a proposed late-game body for transferring stewardship when a campaign’s established shelter network reaches a point where the player cannot personally maintain every site. Its central question is not how to win more territory. It is what can be handed over safely, what must be dismantled, what may remain open without a keeper, and what promises expire when the campaign moves on. The Assembly’s scope is intentionally narrower than a new settlement manager or campaign resolver. It can prepare and witness handoffs; existing site, inventory, expedition, faction, and ending owners determine actual world consequences.

Its provisional places are Farrier’s Last Bridge, Hollow Way Nursery, Low Signal Roof, and Turnback Granary. The Bridge needs repeated structural checks; the Nursery’s future depends on a willing caretaker; the Roof’s signal can be left active but may never receive an answer; and the Granary contains supplies designated for a return that may not happen. The player sees who maintains each site and what work remains before making a handoff offer.

Dema Quill writes task lists with names and dates. Nils Oren wants the receiving community to decide what should grow in the Nursery. Sali Reeve argues that a route can close without the people who used it becoming a failure. Fen Tav wants one chance to repair the Bridge. Mira Selt insists that supplies kept for a return are not automatically abandoned. The Handover Stewards favor reliable transfer. Open Horizon Custodians prefer leaving sites open when safe. Return Route Advocates insist that a future traveler needs honest limits. The Continuance Assembly tries to hold these positions together without acquiring unilateral control.

A five-quest arc starts with an inspection of the Last Bridge and a visible list of unresolved repairs. The player then invites a possible successor, who may refuse; performs a walk-through at the Nursery; decides what can be moved from the Granary using canonical inventory; and records one final route note at the Roof. The culmination offers transfer, preserve with a named review, dismantle safely, leave unclaimed, or postpone closure once. None is universally best. A successor’s refusal remains a legitimate end state and should lead to a practical return plan rather than a persuasion loop.

The proposed mechanic is a stewardship handback packet: site condition, unresolved task, current keeper, receiving party if any, and the date the offer should be reviewed. It must be a projection of existing campaign and site facts, not a parallel legacy ledger. The transfer of people, supplies, keys, or route access must call existing owners. If no owner can persist the selected disposition, keep the choices authored inside the existing endgame quest and do not claim cross-run effects. The UI must show who accepts each obligation, which costs are irreversible, and what is still unknown.

Sample line: “I would rather leave it unclaimed than assign a duty to strangers.” The Assembly succeeds when an ending preserves the difference among transfer, closure, and uncertainty. It fails if every site must be captured, every successor must agree, or a hopeful message is presented as a guarantee. Save round trips, deterministic replay, and an ending projection check are required before implementation. Roll back any new authority that duplicates CampaignLegacySystem or UnifiedEndingResolver, and retain the narrative arc as content if the handoff state has no compatible owner.

### Supplemental packet 01: playable post-ending visits and aftermath coda — Willow Step Depot action 1

A resident asks the player to compare the same word as used by two shelters before calling it agreement. The player sees the cost before accepting and can refuse without losing the ability to return.
