**Location and shelter lore.** Explain who built Mothglass Terrace, what failed there, who repaired it, what custom grew from that repair, and who still pays its cost. Give the player one physical trace, one remembered phrase, one disputed interpretation, and one maintenance task. On a return visit, show the consequence before dialogue summarizes it. A quiet shelter detail should carry history: a bed rotated away from a draft, a cup reserved for visitors, a chalk line refreshed after rain, or a tool returned sharper than it was found.

**Character and faction direction.** The resident speaks plainly and notices labor before symbolism. A witness from **First Return Party** uses formal language until a shortage makes the stakes concrete. A third voice may be an apprentice, courier, absent person represented by an object, or elder who remembers a different version. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive one measurable outcome in the roster, route, archive, relationship, or ending projection.

**Story, UI, and verification.** The side quest needs an entry condition, player action, cost, consequence, refusal branch, archive fact, late-arrival variant, and missing-record variant. Prose should reveal the mechanic through ordinary work. The UI needs a compact label, expanded explanation, focus order, keyboard/controller close and back, readable long text, contrast, non-color cues, and confirmation for irreversible actions. Acceptance requires premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, focused contract or data checks, save round trip, paired deterministic replay, performance notes, and a rollback boundary. The packet is not an implementation claim; it is ready only for a safe-slice review.


## Wave 58 supplemental receipt

The supplemental packets preserve the active twenty-field structure and broaden the playable content bank. They remain provisional until current catalog, ownership, save, replay, UI, accessibility, performance, and rollback evidence is attached.


## Wave 58 extended depth layer

This larger tranche adds six extended packets per plan. They deepen the active twenty fields while keeping all mechanics, catalog rows, factions, locations, shelter customs, and late-game institutions provisional and owner-bound.

### Wave 58 extended depth packet 01: shared-term correction at Mothglass Terrace

#### Extended field 01 — Premise and canon

The shared-term correction begins as a premise audit around Mothglass Terrace. The player is asked to ask two speakers to define the same phrase, but the proposal remains provisional until current source, JSON authority, event producer, host consumer, and ownership ledger are cited. Record the nearest existing seam, the exact absent seam, and the collision to exclude. If the premise is already represented, fold the prose into that owner and retire this packet rather than creating a duplicate.

#### Extended field 02 — Player loop

The loop has six readable beats: arrive at Mothglass Terrace, inspect a practical sign, hear a resident’s account, choose a cost, perform one visible task, and return after the next weather or duty turn. The choice can preserve, delay, redirect, or refuse the request. Show the consequence before explanation. A failure gives information or a bounded recovery task unless the canonical owner defines a terminal result.

#### Extended field 03 — System contract

Route the command through the current owner for playable post-ending visits and aftermath coda. Define command, event key, inputs, output fact, refusal, fallback, idempotency, and consumer. The packet may touch faction standing, route access, roster duty, shelter archive, relationship, expedition, or ending interpretation only through those authorities. It may not create a private truce score, route graph, calendar, inventory, reputation counter, or parallel legacy record.

#### Extended field 04 — Mechanic

Introduce one mechanic that makes maintenance and trust interact: a concession opens a safer task, a late repair changes a route window, or an honest admission reduces a future surprise. The mechanic should have a threshold, a visible cost, a reversible preparation state, and a deterministic result. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk scene before committing to the late-game version.

#### Extended field 05 — Location lore

At Willow Step Depot, describe who built the room, which flood or fire altered it, who kept the key, and why one wall remains unpainted. Give the player a physical trace, a remembered phrase, a disputed interpretation, and a maintenance action. Returning to the site should show an object moved, repaired, withheld, or shared before any dialogue summarizes the change.

#### Extended field 06 — Shelter lore

The shelter projection keeps a custom tied to the same fact: a cup reserved for a messenger, a bell rung only after consent, a cord tied around a tool, or a bench left open for the missing. The custom has a practical function and a social cost. Its archive text must name the worker who sustains it and the person who objects without reducing either voice to exposition.

#### Extended field 07 — Character voices

Write three distinct voices. A resident of Willow Step Depot notices labor and weather. A representative of First Return Party speaks in careful public terms until the cost reaches a family or crew. A witness linked to Keepers of the Last Note remembers a different sequence. Give each a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and late callback. Let a minor voice receive a measurable roster, route, archive, or ending consequence.

#### Extended field 08 — Faction politics

The faction layer distinguishes First Return Party, Keepers of the Last Note, Unfinished Visit Circle, and Afterlight Visitors by resource, ritual, and risk rather than color. First Return Party wants a reliable public record, Keepers of the Last Note protects a route custom, Unfinished Visit Circle values a scarce repair skill, and Afterlight Visitors demands a future witness. None is automatically virtuous. Coalition progress is a projection of existing standing and event facts, with dissent and abstention preserved.

#### Extended field 09 — Story and prose

The side quest opens with an ordinary sentence: someone asks whether the lamp, map, ledger, meal, or signal can wait one more night. The player’s answer changes who performs the task and what is remembered. Use restrained prose, concrete objects, and one silence that another character interprets differently. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants.

#### Extended field 10 — Late-game system

The late-game form is a major faction or frontier institution that can only appear after several owner-bound facts agree. It may convene a coalition, certify a route, steward a shelter custom, or carry a legacy signal. Its powers are bounded: it can request, witness, schedule, or interpret. It cannot rewrite history, bypass save ownership, or silently convert provisional prose into canon.

#### Extended field 11 — Data and catalog

Candidate content rows for shared-term correction carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Link every row to one canonical consumer and one command. Keep Low Bell Harbor, Old Thread Orchard, Unfinished Visit Circle, and Afterlight Visitors provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven.

#### Extended field 12 — Save and migration

Use the smallest existing save section. Capture the new fact, restore it, migrate older envelopes, tolerate an absent optional row, and make duplicate events idempotent. Define the pre-event, committed, refused, interrupted, and restored states. Do not encode prose branches in a panel cache. A rollback note must identify the event boundary and the owner responsible for undo or compensating projection.

#### Extended field 13 — Deterministic replay

Pin seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation. Avoid wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, hidden random choices, and locale-sensitive sorting. Include a late-arrival replay and a missing-record replay so optional content cannot alter the deterministic core unexpectedly.

#### Extended field 14 — UI and accessibility

The UI exposes a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard and controller back behavior, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, and confirmation for irreversible choices. Provide an audio or text alternative. If a record is missing, show a truthful unavailable state and preserve navigation. Archive and map panels consume projections; they do not own decisions.

#### Extended field 15 — Performance and lifecycle

Set budgets for catalog parse, query, event dispatch, archive projection, panel refresh, long text, and return visits. Load high-volume rows lazily, page them without changing order, dispose listeners on close, and avoid repeated full-catalog scans. Add one degradation path for a missing asset or provider. Note the smallest focused host smoke needed if the owner route is eventually implemented.

#### Extended field 16 — Acceptance and handoff

Acceptance requires premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable player command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and a rollback boundary. The handoff names untouched shared paths and labels this as design scaffolding. The final image is practical: a repaired latch, an amended map, a divided bowl, a chalk mark, a quiet signal, or a door left open by consent.

### Wave 58 capsule 01: two definitions remain visible at Mothglass Terrace

**Opening and choice.** At **Mothglass Terrace**, the player finds a practical problem that cannot be solved by rhetoric alone: a weather window is closing, a shared tool has two claimants, a missing person may be returning, a night signal is being misread, an apprentice is ready before the shelter is ready, a water ration has been counted twice, a quiet route carries an old debt, or a legacy object must be placed in another person’s hands. The player inspects the evidence, asks for consent, compares accounts, chooses a cost, defers, or leaves. The cost appears before commitment and a refusal keeps a safe return path.

**Authority and mechanic.** Route the action through the current owner for playable post-ending visits and aftermath coda. Define one command, one event key, one resulting fact, one refusal result, one fallback, and one idempotency rule. A derived readiness view may combine existing standing, relationship, route, roster, shelter, archive, expedition, or ending facts, but it cannot become a second ledger or clock. The mechanic should make an ordinary task consequential: rescheduling a crossing changes who carries a tool, recording a signal changes which watch is asked to stand, or accepting a handover changes who is invited to the next meeting. The player can test the boundary in a low-risk version first.

**Place and shelter lore.** At **Willow Step Depot**, describe the builder, the repair that saved the room, the person who still pays for that repair, and the mark that remains unexplained. At **Low Bell Harbor**, place a contrasting trace: a patched hinge, a dry shelf, an erased route line, a bell rope, a teaching slate, or a bowl set aside. At **Old Thread Orchard**, let a shelter custom make the history useful: a lamp is moved only after consent, a tool is returned sharpened, a guest cup is washed before dawn, or a route name is spoken once and then left unclaimed. Returning to the location shows a changed object before exposition.

**Characters and factions.** A resident speaks in concrete duties and notices who will carry the burden. A representative of **First Return Party** uses public language and wants an auditable result. A voice from **Keepers of the Last Note** protects a custom that looks inefficient until its history is heard. **Unfinished Visit Circle** values a scarce skill, while **Afterlight Visitors** asks who will witness the consequence after the player leaves. Give each voice a promise, fear, boundary, apology, refusal, and callback. The late-game factional version may convene a coalition, certify a passage, steward a shelter custom, or preserve a memory, but it may request and witness only through existing authorities.

**Story and prose.** The scene opens with one quiet sentence about work: “The rope is dry enough for one more crossing,” “The cup was left where the missing person could find it,” or “The bell was rung before anyone agreed.” The player’s response changes who performs the task, what the journal remembers, and which later character feels entitled to speak. Add calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, late-arrival, and missing-record variants. Use concrete objects, short silences, and a callback that makes the earlier mechanic visible without turning the packet into a lore lecture.

**Data and content volume.** Candidate rows carry schema_version, snake_case ID, owner, prerequisites, references, effects, fallback text, localization key, archive policy, retirement note, and missing-data behavior. Create arrival, inspection, task, hazard, rest, departure, return, calm, pressure, failure, recovery, refusal, and late-arrival variants. Keep the names of **First Return Party**, **Keepers of the Last Note**, **Unfinished Visit Circle**, and **Afterlight Visitors** provisional until catalog aliases and reachability are proven. A missing optional row should collapse to a truthful unavailable state rather than alter the deterministic core.

**Persistence and replay.** Capture the smallest new fact through the existing save section. Define pre-action, committed, refused, interrupted, restored, migrated, and duplicate-event states. Pin the campaign seed, event key, input order, and expected projection. Paired replays must agree on standing, access, route, roster, archive, or ending interpretation, including the late-arrival and missing-record cases. Do not use wall-clock seeds, unordered iteration, locale-sensitive sorting, or hidden randomness in prose.

**UI, accessibility, and lifecycle.** Expose a compact action label, expanded explanation, cost, consequence preview, focus order, keyboard/controller close and back, readable long text, contrast, scaling, non-color cues, confirmation for irreversible actions, and text or audio alternatives. Panels consume owner projections and dispose listeners on close. High-volume rows load lazily and page without changing order. Set budgets for parse, query, dispatch, archive projection, refresh, and return visits; document the missing-provider path and the smallest eventual host smoke.

**Acceptance and handoff.** Accept the capsule only with premise evidence, owner and consumer proof, one reachable command, save round trip, migration fixture, paired replay, accessibility review, performance notes, and rollback. The handoff records untouched shared paths and labels the content as design scaffolding. The final image is small and physical: a cord retied, a cup passed over, a map corrected, a signal answered, a tool returned sharper, a meal divided, or a door left open because someone was asked first.

## Wave 58 capsule receipt

The capsule layer remains documentation-only and is ready for premise review, not production promotion.


## Wave 58 playable-content atlas — playable post-ending visits and aftermath coda

This atlas deepens the active twenty-field plan with a new integrated story and mechanics layer. Candidate places, names, systems, and factions are provisional. The separate prose-first Wave 58 plans were indexed but not copied; this atlas avoids their six graffiti and shelter-record anchors. Every stateful proposal below must map to a current owner before implementation.

### Narrative throughline and campaign rhythm

The campaign runs through four movements. At Mothglass Terrace, the player first sees a practical discrepancy rather than a faction banner. At Willow Step Depot, a person explains the cost of leaving it unresolved. At Low Bell Harbor, the player tests one response under low pressure. At Old Thread Orchard, a broader group tries to make that response repeatable and discovers what the first solution failed to address. The final movement returns to the opening object after other residents have had time to act. This rhythm keeps story, task, and consequence joined: a record changes hands, a cup is retested, a task is declined, or a key waits for an accepting custodian.

A major story decision cannot be solved by a single persuasion check. The player may learn, defer, offer help, revise the proposal, leave, or refuse. Each route needs a readable immediate cost and a later callback. Keep emotional resolution separate from mechanical completion: a repaired room does not force forgiveness; a safe water notice does not prove the source permanently safe; a successful trial task does not assign a new job; and a site handoff does not guarantee that the receiving group will continue the same custom.

### System and mechanic design packets

#### Mechanic 01: ending-conditioned optional visit selector from existing ending facts

**Player-facing loop.** At Mothglass Terrace, Aven Marr presents one situation that can be understood by inspection before the player commits. The available responses are to check the evidence, ask the affected person, compare an alternative, perform the bounded task, wait for another party, or decline. The feature should reveal the cost in ordinary terms: time from a shift, a route detour, a limited number of supplies, a public disclosure, or a duty that needs a named replacement. The player must be able to back out before the irreversible step.

**Rule and owner boundary.** The candidate rule is: record only the observable fact the existing quest or domain owner can support; the named faction supplies narrative context, not authority. Derive any display from that fact; never infer consent, safety, reconciliation, assignment, or successful stewardship from silence. Identify the source event, consumer, command, refusal result, fallback, and duplicate-event behavior during premise review. No parallel counter, schedule, route graph, hazard model, biography, game-score store, or ending resolver is authorized. If the live owner lacks the required operation, ship this as authored choice text or leave it blocked.

**Return and verification.** On return, show a changed object or task state before a character explains it. Include calm, scarcity, interruption, late arrival, and missing-data variants. If persistent, test capture/restore, a legacy-save fallback, and same-seed replay; if derived only, verify that the projection does not mutate its source. The UI needs keyboard and controller focus, readable explanation, non-color status cues, and a truthful unavailable state. Accept only when the action produces an observable result and a recoverable refusal path.

#### Quest 01: The First Visit after the Ending

**Opening image.** At Mothglass Terrace, Tavi Reeve finds a physical sign that the previous account is incomplete. The sign is useful but not definitive: a phrase copied two ways, a brace mark older than the load, a rule card with a missing turn, or an epilogue object altered by a new keeper. The first dialogue invites observation and does not presume the player knows which group is right. First Return Party has a practical stake, while another resident bears a different cost.

**Playable sequence.** The player examines the trace, asks one witness a specific question, and performs or declines one bounded action. Offer three authored paths: act now with a known cost, wait for more evidence while accepting delay, or leave the matter unresolved. A failed attempt reveals a new fact or enables recovery. A successful task changes a physical condition or a supported owner projection, then gives the affected person a chance to comment without requiring gratitude.

### Character personality and relationship mini-arcs

#### Character arc 01: Aven Marr

**Established posture.** Aven Marr is a visitor who shares one true detail and refuses to summarize an entire shelter. Show this through a repeated action, not a biography panel: checking a seam, turning a sample strip toward the light, rewriting a public line, pausing before a task, or counting who returned. Their immediate want is to complete one practical responsibility without having someone else define what it means. Their fear is specific to this story and should be stated only when trust and timing make it credible.

**Three playable beats.** First, the player witnesses the character’s skill or boundary at Mothglass Terrace. Second, a pressure event lets the player ask, offer help, or step back; the character can decline without a hidden penalty. Third, a return scene shows the character correcting the player’s assumption or changing their own plan. First Return Party may pressure or support the choice, but it cannot speak for the character. The ending uses existing relationship or quest state only if that owner supports it. Include one line of humor, one line under pressure, one apology, and one boundary statement.

### Scenario and consequence matrix

#### Scenario 01: the selected ending has no data for one optional visit

Run the scene at Mothglass Terrace. Establish what the player knows, what remains uncertain, who bears the cost, and which action can change the situation. Unfinished Visit Circle receives a clear opportunity to state its interest but cannot remove the affected resident’s choice. Outcomes include completed, delayed, refused, interrupted, partially recovered, and optional-content-missing. Show cost before commitment and preserve a safe leave route. The journal or UI reports only the canonical result and names any unresolved portion. ### Return-visit and prose variants

#### Return variant 01: Mothglass Terrace

On a calm return, Sella Orr changes one ordinary object and offers a short update. Under pressure, the same character states the immediate limit first. After refusal, they acknowledge that the player left the choice with them. After a failed task, they reveal one new clue or a safe next step. On late arrival, the person who acted explains what they did before the player arrived; the player is not credited for it. If the relevant record is missing, the scene says the history is unavailable and continues. Keep the callback under a few sentences, use the same underlying facts across audio and text, and avoid turning hardship into a reward.

### Late-game chapter sequence

#### Chapter beat 01: The chosen ending closes

**Chapter purpose.** This chapter moves the player from a local task toward a regional decision without pretending the decision is already supported by the game. At Mothglass Terrace, Dorin Ash raises a concrete complication involving First Return Party. The player first learns what has changed, then chooses whether to ask for another account, spend effort on a practical response, prepare a reversible option, or leave the matter unresolved. The chapter gives one short scene, one playable objective, one optional conversation, and one return callback.

**Branching.** The main path changes only the current owner’s fact. A delayed path reserves the same information for later and explains its opportunity cost. A refusal path preserves the character’s autonomy and does not quietly lower another unrelated score. If the campaign’s actual owner cannot remember this choice, do not invent a new save field: make the outcome local to the authored quest.

**Content and handoff.** Include a location title, objective copy, two lines for each affected voice, a journal summary, a no-audio equivalent, and one environmental cue. The final action should be tangible: check the brace, replace a seal, correct a name, return a key, or mark the uncertainty. The scene sets up the next chapter without promising that its outcome is guaranteed.

## Wave 58 late-game major faction dossier — The Afterlight Visitors

The Afterlight Visitors are a proposed late-game network of guests who return after the main campaign ending to describe what they personally observed. They are witnesses and visitors, not a second governing body and not a device for undoing the ending. Their scenes turn selected campaign consequences into optional playable coda visits: the player can walk, inspect, listen, ask one question, or leave. The coda does not simulate additional campaign days or imply that a hoped-for outcome happened everywhere.

The Visitors appear at Mothglass Terrace, Willow Step Depot, Low Bell Harbor, and Old Thread Orchard. The Terrace supports a short walk and a view of the former departure route. The Depot shows one correction made by a new keeper. Low Bell Harbor allows an arrival without promising a return crossing. Old Thread Orchard shows a custom that has changed while its origin remains visible. The group includes First Return Party, Keepers of the Last Note, Unfinished Visit Circle, and the Afterlight Visitors. Members disagree about whether a final visit should confirm, question, or simply coexist with the ending the player chose.

Aven Marr shares one true detail without summarizing a whole shelter. Kelm Voss prefers a quiet walk to a speech. Nara Pell asks which customs are invitations and which are obligations. Tavi Reeve returns late and complicates the expected epilogue. Sella Orr keeps a room ready without naming its future guest. Five quests offer a first visit, an optional path, a conversation with a new keeper, a contrasting memory, and a final opportunity to end the visit. The player may decline any scene and keep the original ending intact.

The proposed system is a read-only post-ending visit selector driven only by outcome facts the existing ending resolver already owns. Each scene names its prerequisites and neutral fallback. A missing flag must not invent a success, a missing journal record must not block the visit, and coda dialogue cannot revise the resolved ending. If the current scene router has no post-ending path, leave this as a content pack and request an architecture decision; do not make another ending resolver or campaign-save section.

Sample line: “The ending happened. This visit does not change it.” The faction’s late-game influence is that it preserves room for local testimony after a major decision. It cannot recruit the player into renewed play or promise a new chapter. Coda scenes need a skip option, concise recap, safe exit, and text/audio parity. Same-ending saves must show the same factual outcomes regardless of visit order; any variable response must use a deterministic authored condition. Roll back any branch that contradicts the chosen ending, consumes a new campaign day, or creates cross-run rewards.

### Candidate content record 001: a public task can continue after the person who began it leaves the  — Arrival

## Wave 59 late-game major faction dossier — The Long Custody Council

### Charter and origin
The Long Custody Council formed around a dispute that made the plan’s central problem impossible to ignore: pre-ending continuity commitments, bounded handoffs, and a final account of public work. Its founding promise is practical and bounded. It can convene, witness, coordinate, or preserve an agreed practice through current owners. It cannot become the universal authority for diplomacy, routes, shelter occupancy, relationships, or endings. Its founding site, Horizon Steps, contains a visible trace of the first compromise and a separate trace left by someone who refused it. The origin is presented through attributed accounts so the player can compare motives and consequences.

### Internal politics and personalities
The faction contains three live positions: a cautious caucus that prefers local control, an operational caucus willing to accept narrow shared duties, and a dissenting group that worries the charter will outgrow its consent. Use Neri Voss, Eshan Vale, Luma Orr, Perrin Ash as distinct voices, each with a practical skill, a boundary, a reason to refuse the player, and an apology they can make. No member speaks for every shelter. The player can support a pilot, ask for revision, observe, or leave.

### Five-quest arc
1. The invitation: inspect the charter and choose observer status, a pilot, or no affiliation.
2. A task under pressure: a practical request tempts the group to exceed its agreed scope.
3. The absent voice: an affected person asks for a different participation or access path.
4. Review after consequence: the player and faction revisit an observable result without erasing the earlier choice.
5. A right to end: the organization chooses a review condition, sunset, or local return of authority where current owners support it.

Every quest has entry evidence, an action, a result, refusal, missing-data behavior, and a late callback. Keep a quest authored if the current quest graph cannot represent its state.

### Late-game feature and consequence
Its major-faction role is to make regional coordination playable while keeping its limits visible. A final offer can support a local arrangement, a bounded network, or non-affiliation. The result is submitted to existing campaign and faction authorities; the dossier creates no extra ending. Show what the faction accepts, what it cannot promise, and what remains unverified.

### Integration and rollback
Verify the active catalog schema, faction identity, consumer, quest route, save owner, deterministic event path, UI lifecycle, and exact path claims before implementation. Require a focused route check, replay for deterministic state, save round trip for persistence, accessibility review, and measured performance for the changed path. Rollback disables only the new faction entry and invitation route; ordinary campaign play, local groups, and existing factions remain intact.

## Wave 59 collision and premise review

### Review gate 01

Existing faction identity or standing may already cover the invitation. Search live IDs and consumers before adding a new row.

### Review gate 02

An integrated or partial quest can already own the scene entry or callback. Check plan indexes and current quest data.

### Review gate 03

Shelter occupancy, privacy, rest, lighting, or access may have a current owner. Reuse only matching semantics.

### Review gate 04

Campaign manifest and ending history remain authoritative; never add a shadow completion flag.

### Review gate 05

Data schema may differ from a proposal. Validate references, ranges, localization, and consumer reachability.

### Review gate 06

Older or partial saves need the existing save owner and a safe default before stateful promotion.

### Review gate 07

An unverified location label is design text, not a stable catalog ID. Resolve its map and travel route first.

### Review gate 08

A UI callback cannot become a gameplay authority; find the canonical command/event seam.

### Review gate 09

An optional content row must not block the ordinary route when its character or prerequisite is missing.

### Review gate 10

If the feature needs a new registry, clock, route graph, occupancy model, or ending resolver, stop for an architecture decision.

## Wave 59 closeout receipt

Wave 59 adds passes 637–647, ten numbered design fields per pass, 200 candidate content records, twelve story packets, location and shelter lore, feature specifications, character personalities, UI/UX and performance gates, integration bridges, and the late-game major faction The Long Custody Council. The separate prose-first Wave 59 index was used for anchor avoidance; its indexed candidate material was not copied. This is a documentation-only design wave. No code, authoritative game data, tests, or ownership claims changed.

## Wave 60 closeout — endgame convergence integration course

### Closeout disposition

Plan 16 closes as a proposed endgame layer that asks who maintains public works, stores community knowledge, and takes responsibility for unfinished obligations after the campaign's major crisis. The Long Custody Council is a provisional faction concept. Its late-game availability and legacy outcomes must be authored as consequences of existing campaign facts, not as a parallel endgame simulator, hidden score, or replacement ending system.

The player should encounter convergence through small, legible callbacks: a repaired relay still carries a community's evacuation instructions; an earlier faction agreement determines who can use a storehouse; a survivor chooses whether to preserve a name in a public register. These scenes should reward remembered actions without making one early choice silently close unrelated content. Missing optional flags should resolve to a stable neutral line and a valid ending route.

### Evidence boundary and dependency order

The repository contains a campaign completion history owner and extensive existing ending-continuity work. That evidence supports a careful audit of available campaign facts; it does not prove that every Plan 16 flag is captured by the current completion snapshot. The global Plan 17 environmental storytelling plan and multiple continuity/endgame plans are indexed, so callbacks and locations need a collision pass before new content is authored.

### Integration course

1. **Trace campaign facts.** Review current completion-history capture, save/restore, ending input construction, campaign flags, faction standing, quest outcomes, and indexed endgame plans. For each proposed callback, record the real producer, canonical owner, persistence boundary, and consumer. Remove callbacks with no live producer or reader.
2. **Define a narrow convergence matrix.** Use a short table of prerequisite facts and authored variants. Missing, unknown, and false facts must be distinguishable where the current source provides those meanings. Do not add a generic fact registry just to simplify the table.
3. **Author one complete late-game slice.** The MVP is one accessible location, one short quest or discovery, two or three dialogue variants, and one post-crisis record entry. Require no more than one mandatory prior quest. Offer a fallback for an absent companion, faction, or location.
4. **Preserve ending ownership.** The existing ending owner remains authoritative for terminal resolution. New content contributes through a supported campaign fact or authored narrative observation; it does not select endings directly from a UI callback.
5. **Persist only real durable facts.** Use the owning quest, faction, relationship, discovery, or campaign-completion save section. Capture/restore and migration need to be specified before any new durable field is introduced. Keep transient selection and presentation state transient.
6. **Verify every path.** With a current claim, run the focused content, campaign continuity, save migration, and determinism checks selected by the integrator. Exercise fresh campaign, all relevant earlier outcomes, missing prerequisite, optional location absence, load before/after convergence, and terminal route. Run Godot headless only if runtime presentation or map routing changed.

### Candidate impact map, risks, and completion test

Candidate premise-review paths include Assets/Ashfall.Core/Endgame/CampaignCompletionHistory.cs, the current campaign and quest authorities, the existing ending context owner, location discovery and faction standing owners, relevant canonical data, and the existing journal/map host surfaces. These are candidate read paths, not claims. Shared ownership and active worktree claims remain decisive.

Risks are missing campaign facts, endgame content that unexpectedly blocks completion, save schemas that cannot distinguish an old save from a negative choice, and late branches that are impossible to regression-test. Keep callback prerequisites optional unless they are already part of critical progression; use an explicit unknown/default variant; and require migration evidence before adding persisted facts. Roll back by withdrawing the catalog reference and retaining saved fields that existing saves may contain.

The course is complete when every callback has a traced producer and consumer, all missing-data routes remain playable, the existing ending authority still owns resolution, saved outcomes survive supported migration, replay is stable, and focused verification plus an integration handoff are recorded. This document records no implementation completion.
